W. A. Bird was shot in the shoulder, the ball passing entirely through him and coming out near the spinal cord. Bird is 30 years old and unmarried.

Col. Thomas G. Jones, of the 2d regiment Alabama State troops, arrived here this morning with five companies and is confident of his ability to prevent any further attempt at mob violence. There was much excitement for a while last night, but it had subsided somewhat today.

ARREST OF THE SHERIFF.

Sheriff Smith has been arrested on the charge of murder.

MILITARY POWER ALONE REPRESSES THE ANGRY PASSIONS OF THE PEOPLE.

BIRMINGHAM, Dec. 10.—There is a forced calm in Birmingham to-day. At 3 o'clock this afternoon the funeral of Postmaster Thockmorton occurred. As he was one of the most popular men in Birmingham, it was feared there would be trouble. It was the largest funeral ever seen here, but passed off without any attempt at violence. There were six others buried in Birmingham to-day and two bodies were shipped to their relatives.

By order of Mayor B. A. Thompson all the saloons were closed till further orders. His authority is questioned and more than one suit was filed for damages.

The dead are Mr. B. Throckmorton, J. R. McCoy, A. B. Tarrant, A. D. Bryant, C. C. Tate, Charles Jenkins, G. H. Brendue, F. White, colored, Colbert Smith and one unknown, J. W. Gilmore and A. J. Schide will not live. Twenty-seven men are badly but not seriously wounded.

Chief of Police Pickard said that he advised against firing on the people, and that it was disgraceful. Mayor Thompson disclaims having given orders to Sheriff Smith to fire. Sheriff Smith, Nat Stanley and several others are under arrest, charged with murder.

THE JAIL

is guarded by military companies from Montgomery, Anniston and Tuscalousa, Col. Thos. G. Jones, in command, has telegraphed Governor Seay asking that prisoners R. R. Hawes and Joseph Smith be removed to Montgomery or else that the military be relieved. A petition signed by over a thousand names has been sent to the Governor, asking to have. Sheriff Smith removed from office, Governor Seay will arrive in Birmingham to-night.

THE CORONER'S JURY

in the Hawes case met to-day and looked at the body of Mrs. Hawes, but adjourned until to-night. May Hawes was buried to-day, the money raised being enough to buy a lot. Lakeview Lake is being drawn off to look for the body of Irene Hawes. A jury has been impanelled over the body of A. D. Bryant, killed on Saturday night at the jail.

SMITH IN MORE DANGER THAN HAWES.

All is quiet so long as the military is kept here, but there will surely be more trouble from the people if they are removed. The people are very angry, but the cannon at the four corners keep them from making any attempt to mob any one. If they were to get in the jail Hawes would be overlooked, but Sheriff Smith would come in for more than would be pleasant.

Ex-Sheriff Sam Truss is put in charge while Joe Smith is held for trial. If Irene's body should be found to-night there may be more serious trouble.

MORE LYNCHING.

There comes news from Gadsden that there is a mob there to lynch a negro who killed a policeman yesterday. Troops may be sent there to-night. They have been asked for.

BIRMINGHAM PARALYZED.

All the jurors will meet to-night. Birmingham has hardly begun to realize what has happened in the last two days. The reaction will be horrible. No business was done to-day.

DYING WORDS OF THE VICTIMS OF THE RIOT.

Birmingham, Ala, December 10.—It is reported that Hawes, who has been the cause of Saturday night's tragedy, has made a full confession of the crimes charged against him.

The following are statements from several men who were near the front of the crowd when the volley was fired:

C. C. Tate, who was mortally wounded, said: "I went up to see what the crowd was going to do. I don't think they would have tried to break the door down, but they might. I did not think the officers would shoot."

A. J. Brannan, deputy United States marshal from Gadsden, now dead, said: "I went there out of curiosity and to see the lynching, if there was one. I did not expect to take part in it."

Matt Kennedy, who is badly wounded, said: "I was there begging the crowd to go back. I had friends in the crowd and did not want them to do anything rash. I wanted law and order maintained, and was doing all I could to that end. I did not think the officers would shoot unless an attack was actually made on the jail."

W. E. Vaughn, a lawyer, said: "I had just left the jail. I met the crowd and pleaded with them to go back. I told them time and again the officers would shoot. They had no leaders, but just before the shooting several men, who were drunk, pressed to the front and said, 'Tear the jail down and hang Hawes.' Then the volley was fired."

All thoughts of attempting any further attacks on the jail were abandoned upon the arrival of the troops ordered here by Governor Seay, although a crowd of curious people stood all day forming a line across 21st street and 2d avenue, where the military guard was formed. The first troops to arrive were the Blues and the Grays and the artillery from Montgomery, who reached the city at 10 o'clock a.m., and were at once marched to the Court House and assigned to their posts of duty. Sentinel lines were established upon all streets leading to the jail, from one to two blocks distant, and no one has since been allowed to approach nearer than that, to the building, unless provided with passes. Of the wounded at the hospital it is now hoped that all will recover. J. W. Gilmore and Matt Kennedy, who are most desperately wounded, are resting quietly. ITEMS OF INTEREST.
Col. E. B. C. Cash, the noted South Carolina duelist, died last Saturday, of paralysis, at the age of 66 years.

Trenton, N. J., has a beautiful young girl, a somnambulist, who perambulates the public streets in her night dress.

The Union Square Theatre, one of the oldest and most valuable playhouses in New York, was destroyed by fire last Tuesday.

Hutchinson & Co., the most prominent merchants of Point Pleasant, made an assignment last week. Liabilities $30,000; assets $8,000.

Commodore Barron, a distinguished officer of the United States and Confederate navies, died in Essex county, Va., last Sunday, aged 80 years.

George Robinson, a colored man, was arrested in Frederick, Md., last Thursday night for an attempted assault on a white woman. Threats of lynching were made.

In Walker county, Ga., Friday, Jeff McGoodan and Taylor Kemp got into a quarrel over a woman, when the former shot the latter through the heart, killing him instantly.

Harry Harwood died in Baltimore last Friday from injuries received by being thrown by his horse in the Ivy City steeplechase last October. He was a noted horseman.

The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad Company, through President Spencer, asks Baltimore for an extension of the five million loan. It is also proposed to wipe out the sinking fund.
Fitz, owned by C. W. Littlejohn, of Leesburg, Va., was awarded the special prize as the best pointer dog on exhibition at the Westminster Kennel Club show in New York.

A few days ago a farmer in Accomac county, Va., found a considerable sum of money in gold and silver coins, supposed to have been buried during the Revolutionary war by a wealthy Englishman.

The National Opera Company "busted" in Washington last week. The expenses were so much greater than the receipts that the company disbanded for good, some of the members being left without a cent.

Joseph H. Beeler, a prominent citizen of Greencastle, Pa., aged fifty-six years, committed suicide Monday by hanging himself to a rafter in the garret of his house. His wife died some time ago, leaving him with four small children, and grief over his loss drove him insane.

All of the engineers and firemen on the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad went on a strike at 4 o'clock Monday morning. They want equality in wages, which the company refuses to grant. Very few trains are being run on the road, and its business is almost entirely stopped.

Tolbert Rollins, a crazy man, residing in Perre county, Ark., recently took a novel method of committing suicide. He emptied a powder flask in his mouth and then ignited the powder with a match. The explosion tore away a portion of his face, causing injuries from which he cannot recover.

Three members of the family of Jacob Laing, of Newark, N. J., were made dangerously ill from the effects of drinking tea made of jimson weed, taken by mistake for boneset tea. Mrs. Laing, an aged lady, when first under the influence of the poison, laughed continually; Mrs. Edwards, a married daughter, cried bitterly, and Miss Laing, age 25, became very voluble.

Monmouth, Ill., was startled by a terrific roar or explosion Wednesday night which shook the walls and windows of many buildings in the city. The sky was lit up with what appeared to have been a monster meteor. The direction was from southeast to northwest. Reports from neighboring towns show that all experienced the same sensations to the shock and flight of the visitor.

Boils, pimples, hives, ringworm, tetter, and all other manifestations of impure blood are cured by Hood's Sarsaparilla.

The Mississippi River Commission. The Mississippi River Commission held the first day's session of their annual meeting yesterday in the New York Hotel. Gen. C. D. Comstock, the recently appointed President, was in the chair. Major B. M. Hourd, of Louisiana; Gen. Ferguson, Mississippi, and Prof. Davidson, San Francisco, members of the commission, were present, Col. Suter, Major Ernst and Judge Taylor being absent. Senator E. C. Walthall and Congressman T. C. Catchings, Mississippi, and Senator Eustis, Louisiana, were also present. Capt. James Byrnes, of the Lee Line, will appear before the commission this morning and testify as to the depth of channel at Plum Point. He will be followed by various other steamboat men. The meeting will last several days, and quite a number of residents of Arkansas, Tennessee and Mississippi are in New York to attend. Met Death in Saving a Woman's Life.
HYDE PARK, Mass., Sept. 21. — Patrick Tracey, baggagemaster at the Hyde Park station of the Old Colony Railroad, was struck and instantly killed by a train, yesterday afternoon. He was attempting to save the life of Mrs. Young, aged sixty-nine, of Sharon, who had fallen upon the track, and he had partially succeeded in pulling her from the track when he was struck by the engine. Mrs. Young was fatally injured. Tracey, who was sixty years of age, leaves a widow and three children.

Whites and Negroes Fighting.

SPECIAL TO THE WORLD.

GADSDEN, Ala., Sept. 21.—Sunday night a fight occurred between George Whitt (white) and a colored laborer. Monday night Whitt and his friends fired on five negroes from ambush, killing two and wounding the other three. Later in the night some negroes armed themselves and a battle between the two parties followed. Several are reported killed and wounded on both sides.

Lively Shooting Between Whites and Blacks in Alabama. [Copyright, 1888, by the California Associated Press.]

GADSEN, September 21st.—A fight occurred between George Whitt, white, and a colored laborer. Whitt and his friends fired on five negroes from an ambush, killing two and wounding the other three. Later the negroes armed themselves and a battle between the two parties followed. Several are reported killed and wounded on both sides.

THROUGH THE SOUTH.
Events Of All Sorts Throughou Dixie.
Alabama.
John Davis, a negro miner, was jailed at Birmingham Tuesday. He is suffering from a peculiar malady or hallucination. At sight of a dog or a cat he is taken with a fit and bites at everything in reach, all the time growling and snarling like an angry dog. It was at first thought that he had hydrophobia, but after an examination, physicians say not. He is perfectly sane and in good health, so long as he does not see a cat or a dog. If a dog comes near him he becomes so violent that it is necessary to chain him for several hours. A number of physicians have examined him, but they have so far failed to ascertain the cause of his peculiar malady.

A second bloody race conflict has occurred at Round Mountain, Cherokee county. A special from Gadsden says that on Sunday night a fight occurred between George Whitt, white, and a colored laborer. Monday night Whitt and his frienes fired on five negroes from ambush, killing two and wounding the other three. Later in the night some negroes armed themselves and a regular battle between the two parties followed. Several are reported killed and wounded on both sides.

The negroes of Tuscaloosa are in a terrible fright and meet every night to pray for deliverance from the voudoo. Their meetings often last all night. Flora Baker, a respectable colored woman, owned two horses. On Sunday they suddenly became sick and died a few hours later. Flora said they had been voudooed, and had their stomachs opened. In the stomach of one was found a green snake eight inches long, while the stomach of the other one contained two small lizards. The negroes of the town at once became greatly alarmed, fearing some great harm would come to them through the unknown and mysterious voudoo.

At a negro dance house, in Birmingham, Charley Harris walked up behind Ed Hannilton and shot him through the body, inflicting a fatal wound. Hamilton was dancing with Harris's girl. The murderer escaped.

Tennessee.

A daring robbery is reported from Smith county. Early Tuesday afternoon John Smith, Jr., a contractor on the Nashville and Knoxville railroad, started to Lancaster to pay off his employes. He took with him about $1,000, and was accompanied by his book-keeper, a young man named Shiner. Before the two reached Lancaster they were stopped by two men who caught their horse by the bridle, presented pistols and demanded Mr. Smith's money. Smith refused to give it, and two shots were fired at him. The first missed him, but the second struck his forehead, crushing his skull in. In the meantime Shiner had hurriedly left.

The robbers, after striking Smith and knocking him out of his buggy, took the bag containing the money and fled. Mr. Smith regained consciousness and made his way to the place at which his men were at work. He sent them in pursuit of the robbers and telephoned for bloodhounds. Johnson, one of the employes, took a double-barrel shotgun and started out alone. About four miles from the scene of the robbery he came in sight of the two men, who at once fired upon him. Johnson returned the fire, fatally wounding one and seriously wounding the other. Mr. Johnson recovered the money and took it and the two prisoners to Gordonville. He then secured a wagon, brought the prisoners to Carthage and had them committed to jail.

There was much excitement for a time, and threats of lynching the robbers were indulged in, but when it was learned that the robbers and would-be murderers were wounded more seriously than Mr. Smith, the intense feeling was allayed. One of the robbers is named Charles Rice; the other is a Frenchman, whose name has not been learned. Both have been at work for Mr. Smith, and quit a few days ago on pretense of going to Florida.

James Hunter, a prominent stock dealer living four or five miles west of Midway, committed suicide Tuesday by shooting himself through the heart. He had exhibited signs of insanity for several days, and Monday had a lawyer with him arranging his business. About five years ago his wife was shot and killed while sitting by his side in her own parlor by some unknown person, and ever since that time Hunter has suffered at times from mental aberration.

SOUTHERN GLEANINGS.
The damage to North Carolina cotton by floods is estimated at fifteen per cent.

The dumping of four hundred yellow fever refugees at Hendersonville, N. C., has caused much uneasiness in Charleston, S. C., as quite a number of Charlestonians have summer homes in that neighborhood.

The cotton factors of Savannah, Ga., have organized a pool to fight the Bagging Trust by importing the covering of last year's cotton and using it in place of syndicate bagging. Samples of old covering have been secured and the plan is pronounced practicable. Since the organization of the pool, syndicate bagging has been offered at one-quarter to one-half cent less than quotations.

Two men named Steele and Mockabee, both drunk, boarded a train at Mt. Sterling, Ky., a few days since and fought all the way to Stepstone, where the conductor, for the safety of those in his charge, put the men off and told them to fight it out. They drew pistols and exchanged five shots each. The fifth shot from Steele's pistol passed through Mockabee's brain, killing him instantly. They were cousins. After the killing Steele boarded the train and proceeded home, the train having waited until the duel was over.

At a special election recently the citizens of Augusta, Ga., voted an extra levy of one per cent, to repair the damages to the city caused by the recent floods.

J. B. Bobb, a prominent citizen of Trenton, Ky., while engaged in a mill, a few days ago, had one of his hands cut off with a circular saw. His suffering was so great that there was fear of lock jaw.

The survivors of the Jones and Green families of Hancock County, who have been at war since last February, were placed on trial at Sneedville, Tenn., for murder. Every citizen going into the town was searched. Fifty special deputies were standing guard about the courthouse.

The jury in the case of ex-Secretary of State Will A. Strong, of Louisiana, charged with embezzling about $3,500 from the State, agreed upon a verdict. The sheriff went out to call the Attorney-General, and Strong walked out behind him, attracting no attention. He was declared guilty, but is not to be found.

Louis Hill, a negro fugitive from Union County, Miss., was arrested near Memphis, Tenn., recently, by the sheriff of Union County, who came upon him accidentally. Five years ago Hill resolved to get rid of his wife in order to wed a dusky belle who had enslaved him, and tried to poison her by boiling a moccasin snake's head in her coffee.

A partly-constructed bridge over a ravine in the southern part of Paducah, Ky., gave way a few days ago, and five carpenters—W. F. Brown, J. L. House, H. Palien, Robertson and Roberts—were severely hurt by falling twenty-five feet. John Bachman, who was standing on the bridge watching the men at work, was caught between the timbers and fatally injured, both legs being broken and his head crushed.

The negroes of Tuscaloosa, Ala., are in a terrible fright and meet every night to pray for deliverance from the voodoo. Their meetings often last all night. Flora Baker, a respectable colored woman, owned two horses. A few days since these suddenly became sick and died a few hours later. Flora said they had been voodooed and had their stomachs opened. In the stomach of one was found a green snake eight inches long, while the stomach of the other one contained two small lizards. The negroes of the town at once became greatly alarmed, fearing some great harm would come to them through the unknown and mysterious voodoo.

M. V. Ingram, of Clarksville, Tenn., has issued a call for a meeting of the tobacco planters of the State, to be held In Clarksville on the 20th inst., to take action on the proposition to head off the Regie monopolies and secure full value for the very large crop of tobacco now
in Clarksville on the 20th inst., to take action on the proposition to head off the Regie monopolies and secure full value for the very large crop of tobacco now being housed. The planters will be asked to sign an agreement pledging themselves not to plant any tobacco next year, on condition that a general organization of planters is effected to this end before the 1st of February next.

A fight occurred between George Whitt (white) and a colored laborer at Gadsden, Ala., a few nights ago. Whitt and his friends fired on five negroes from ambush, killing two and wounding the three others. Later in the night negroes armed themselves, and a regular battle between the two parties followed. Several are reported killed and wounded.

There was a strange stew in a church in Burke County, N. C., recently. People who had occasion to enter the building were horrified at seeing a dead man lying on the floor, and beside him a bottle of liquor. An investigation of the case was at once begun, and a most disgraceful state of affairs was brought to light. The dead man was Horace Cardwell, and, in company with two other abandoned fellows, John Mitchell and Columbus Mitchell, he had gone to the church to have a drunken spree. The three had purchased five quarts of brandy, and in a night drank it all save half a pint. When daylight came the Mitchells left. Cardwell lay unconscious on the floor. He never awoke, and was found horribly swollen and distorted. The men had lighted the lamps in the church and had a regular orgy.

As John Smith, stone contractor of the Nashville & Knoxville railroad, and his book-keeper, Mr. Spriner, were between Gordonville and Lancaster, Tenn., a few days ago, on their way to pay off the hands, they were stopped by two men, who demanded the $1,000 which they had in a grip-sack. They fired at the robbers, but Smith was struck on the head and rendered insensible and Springer fled. The robbers escaped with the money, but were soon overtaken in the woods by a party of railroad men, who had been notified by Smith as soon as he recovered consciousness. One of the pursuers named Johnson mortally wounded one of the robbers

A BRAVE WOMAN.
SHE CLIMBS INTO A BELFRY AND RINGS AN ALARM.
A. Sensational Incident-The Broken Raleigh Bank-Escape of Prisoners from Jail.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

RALEIGH, August 10.—An item published in to-day's press dispatches from Chicago stated that Thomas M. Hines, the defaulting cashier of the Atlantic and North Carolina railroad, was arrested there. It was learned to-day that Hines was merely an agent of the road at the little station of Newport and had stolen some $200. Governor Scales today telegraphed the Chief of Police at Chicago to hold Hines.

Two escaped convicts, Sylvester Holloman and Bob Thompson (both colored), have been captured near Wilson.

It is ascertained that the fire at Windsor, Bertie county, burned fully seven thousand dollars' worth of property. A very gallant deed was done by Tabitha Sheppard, who during the fire in the dark climbed into the belfry and rang the church bell to arouse the slumbering people.

Yesterday evening lightning struck and fired a large barn belonging to W. A. Smith, of Ansonville.

The Knights of Labor will meet at Wilson to-morrow for the purpose of nominating candidates for county offices. A sensational incident is reported to have occurred near Wilmington. Late at night a buggy in which were a white man and a woman was stopped near the suburbs by a white man, who commanded the woman to alight. Upon her touching the ground he gave her a terrible beating with a rawhide whip, while her male companion drove away at top speed. After beating the woman the man ordered her home and followed her into the city.

There are not a few people who now believe that there will be another sensation in connection with the State National Bank smash. It is whispered here and there that there will be some indictments in the Federal Court here growing out of this peculiarly sensational case. There is talk all over the State about the matter, and much of it is very harsh indeed. There is no telling what will result. The Treasury Department expert, whose name is Drummond, is still here making a fresh investigation. As yet nothing startling has been developed.

By the end of October the grading of the Murphy branch of the Western North Carolina railroad will be completed beyond Red-Marble gap. There were some months ago complaints of slowness in the construction of that part of the railway. There was a change of route, it appears, which necessitated much new work.

The Republican Congressional Convention of the First district is called at Edenton on the 22d instant by E. A. White, chairman of the Executive Committee.

There is no end of good news of Judge Fowle's canvass. He is working earnestly. He has large audiences and there is no abatement of enthusiasm.

A LYNCHING.

News has been received of the lynching of an unknown white man, supposed to be from Yancey county, by five negroes in Henderson county. A negro named Henry Sumner has told the story of the affair. It is as follows: Two white men met three negro women, one of whom—Lottie Corpening—is a notorious prostitute. From some cause or other the men had a quarrel with the women, which finally resulted in the knocking down of the Corpening woman by one of the men. All three of the women then set upon the men, one of whom fled and made his escape. His companion could not get away and was being beaten unmercifully, when five negro men came up. They set upon the man, and after beating him into insensibility went to a house near by and returned with a rope. The white man was then taken away by the negroes and has not been seen or heard of since. One of the negroes has told another negro that the party "treated him like they treated that negro over in Asheville."

All the negroes have been arrested and jailed at Hendersonville. Their names are William Carpening, John Ramsey, George King, Abraham King, and Henry Sumner, the latter being a witness of the affair.

Considerable excitement exists in Henderson over the matter. A searching party has been organized, and the woods and creeks of that vicinity are being searched for the body of the missing man.

A SENSATION.
AN UNKNOWN BODY DISCOVERED IN THE FRENCH BROAD.
Supposed to be the Man that was Lynched by Negroes in Henderson County.
A ripple of excitement was created upon our streets yesterday by a rumor which was circulated early in the morning to the effect that the body of an unknown white man had been seen floating down that stream by a couple of colored women, who were fishing along the banks of the river. This was about nine o'clock, and Chief of Police F. N. Waddell was immediately notified. In company with police officer Hampton, the Chief at once went to the river, and instituted a search for the floating body, but without success.

William Lyda and Noah Weldon, both colored men, also saw the body, and stated that it was floating face-up, and the arms had the appearance of being tied down to the trunk. It was in the middle of the stream, about halfway between Smith's bridge and the railroad bridge when they saw it. They had no boat; the water in the river was up and running at the rate of seven miles an hour, hence they made no attempt at a rescue, knowing that it would prove futile. The body was also seen by a young white man named Davis, and he corroborated the darkies' statement, in all respects, save that the arms and hands were sticking up out of the water instead of having the appearance of being tied down to the body.

An hour or so later a party of men secured a boat, and going down the river, endeavored to overtake and secure the body. They worked laboriously for several hours, and finally came in view of the floating body as it went over the shoals and went into deep water, about five miles north of the city. The men returned to the city, after seeing that all hope of securing the body was exhausted from this source, and Chief Waddell immediately telegraphed to the authorities at Alexanders, Hot Springs and Marshall to keep a sharp lookout for, and secure the body, if it drifted to either of those places. Up to the hour of going to press last night no news had been received from either of the places, and a searching party will be organized by Chief Waddell this morning to go in search of the body, which is supposed to have been caught in over-hanging brushwood, or drifted upon one of the numerous sand-bars in the French Broad. Considerable interest is manifested in the matter, and the recovery and identity of the body is a matter of much moment to the legal authorities. The discovery will probably be made this morning.

NORTH CAROLINA.
NEWS FROM ALL PARTS OF THE STATE.
A Colored Fair to be Held—Fatal Stabbing—
Requisition from South Carolina—
The Cotton-Bagging Trust, Etc.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
N. G. August 24 — It

BALLEIGH, N. C., August 24.—It has been decided to hold a Colored State Fair here during the week beginning September 25th. Governor Scales will formally open the fair. Addresses will be delivered by Senator Vance and Charles Emory Smith, of the Philadelphia Press. Both Fowle and Dockery have been invited to make speeches during the fair.

Governor Scales left this evening for Greensboro' to join his family, and will remain there this week.

The convict force have completed the grading on the short cut of the Wilmington and Weldon railway to its present terminus at Plainview, and has been transferred to the Cape Fear and Yadkin-Valley railway near Fayetteville.

FATALLY STABBED.

Near Asheville Berry Teague cut John Carver, it is supposed fatally. Carver was completely disembowelled, and also stabbed in the heart. Teague was arrested. He was suffering severely from a blow on the head inflicted by Carver.

H. A. Watkins & Brother, of Winston, have assigned. Liabilities and assets unknown.

A MYSTERIOUS CORPSE IN THE FRENCH BROAD.

The body of a white man has been seen floating in French Broad river near Asheville. It was being carried by a swift current. The hands appeared as if they had been tied to the side of the body. It is the current belief that the body is that of the white man who was recently lynched by negroes in Henderson county for an alleged assault upon a negro woman.

SUDDEN DEATH.

William Nelson, master of the steamer Fanita, of the Clyde Line, plying between New York and Wilmington, died suddenly at Wilmington yesterday of apoplexy. His death was primarily due to over-exertion in New York some days ago.

Sheriff Dawson, of Pamlico county, has caused somewhat of a sensation by failure to account for $1,500 of taxes which he had collected.

The first bale of this season's cotton received here came in this morning. It was grown by Daniel Thomas (colored), of Johnston county, and is considered earlier than that of last season.

NEWBERNE PEOPLE ANGBY.

The people of Newberne are very angry about a telegram which was sent to Mayor E. H. Meadows from Goldsboro', and signed John B. Baird, Washington, D. C. It was as follows:

"If you and the advertising fool-doctors dare to stop the train fifty miles from Morehead City Monday wire me, and I will bring men enough from Goldsboro', La Grange, and Kinston to raise your quarantine." A number of men are mad at the folly of Baird, who is said to have a position in the Post-Office Department at Washington, D. C., and the Postmaster-General and President Cleveland have been officially informed of his conduct. Last night he went down to the quarantine station, this side of Newberne, where he met Mayor Meadows. He denied sending the telegram as it was received. The City Council will demand a full apology from Baird, who is certainly in hot water.

MEMORIAL MONUMENTS.

Subscription lists for the fund for putting headstones at the graves of the North Carolina dead in Hollywood cemetery are now being opened at a number of points in this State. Governor Scales is now more hopeful of securing the desired amount.

The monument on Mt. Mitchell to the memory of the late Professor Mitchell, of Chapel Hill, has been completed, thanks to the filial devotion of his nephew. It required a month's hard labor to transport to the mountain-top the materials for the monument, each piece having to be carried by mountaineers. Mt. Mitchell is the highest peak east of the Mississippi. Professor Mitchell lost his life there.

JUTE BAGGING.

Experiments are being made with all sorts of substitutes for jute bagging. The farmers have gone earnestly into the matter, and say they will do what they can to block the game of the trust. The Alliance is officially spreading the news, and of course this secures a remarkable unanimity of action otherwise unattainable.

Goldsboro's alleged yellow-fever patient is now well, and amuses himself hunting squirrels. He is yet quarantined.

Brower thinks that he has practically whipped out the Republican Executive Committee of the Fifth district.

COTTON-SEED OIL AND COTTON.

The farmers of Edgecombe county are building a cotton-seed-oil mill at Shiloh. It will be co-operative.

Cotton is beginning to open. The nights are very cool and will do some injury, of course, causing dropping of squares and bolls. But the outlook is very favorable.

A committee on the part of the stockholders of the Cape Fear and Yadkin-Valley railroad is making a thorough inspection of that line.

SILK-MILLS.

The capacity of the new silk-mills at Wadesboro' is to be considerably increased. The shipments of silk so far have been 1,600 pounds. Electricity is to be used for lighting the mills.

Burglars are again very daring at Wilmington. Night before last one was shot twice and very badly injured.

The farmers' alliances are falling in line and denouncing the cotton-bagging trust.

The committee appointed to consider the question of the removal of the site of the Grand Lodge of Masons from Raleigh to Oxford is to meet at Geensboro' Monday to consider the matter. G. W. Blount is chairman of the committee.

jerry-long-washington-1888-05-19.A1:
A DASTARDLY OUTRAGE.
Four Negroes Assault a White Woman and Her Little Daughter.
CHATTANOOGA, Tenn., May 18.—The most horrible outrage ever heard of in Tennessee occurred last night in the northern portion of Rhea county. Mrs. Rice, a respectable white widow with three children, was hunting work in the neighborhood of Kenrick ore mines. Failing to secure a lodging place she went into a vacant house near the mines to stop for the night. About 10 o'clock four negroes, James Strickland, Nick Webster, Jerry Long and Sam Sibner broke open the door and forced the poor woman to submit to their desires at the point of the revolver. They afterward drove her away from her children, and during her absence injured her twelve-year-old girl shamefully. This morning at 4 o'clock Mrs. Rice went to the house to get her children when the four brutes attacked her again. They subsequently fled, but were soon captured by officers and lodged in the jail at Washington this afternoon. A special received tonight says Mrs. Rice has identified each of the scoundrels, and that a mob will lynch them tonight or tomorrow night. The whole county is up in arms over the crime.
jerry-long-washington-1888-05-19.A2:
Quadruple Lynching.
CHICAGO, May 19.—A special from Spring City, Tennessee, says it is reported four negro laborers have been lynched near Worthington for outraging a white woman a couple of nights ago.
jerry-long-washington-1888-05-19.A5:
TENNESSEE.
Information has just reached Chattanooga of a terrible crime committed Thursday in Rhea county by four negroes, three of whom have been captured and lodged in the county jail at Washington. The four negroes went to a white widow womans' house, and two of them brutally outraged her, while the other two attempted to criminally assault her daughter. In this, however, they failed, the girl eluding them and escaping, gave an alarm, which drew some neighbors some distance away, to their assistance. All four of the negroes ran, but a large posse was soon raised and going in pursuit captured three of them, as stated. Parttes from that section, which is remote from the telegraph and railroad, who came down the river to Chattanooga say that if the parties arrested prove to be the guilty men, there's sure to be a quadrupple lynch ing in the county of Rhea within the next few days. The name of the white woman assaulted could not be learned.

Friday, at Chattanooga, Jasper Bates shot his mother-in-law, Ann Smith, through the right hand and right leg, inflicting dangerous wounds. His wife had just given birth to a child, and he went to the trunk and got a revolver and was approaching the bed with it when his mother-in-law grabbed the weapon and the shooting followed. Bates is in jail on a charge of shooting with intent to kill.

An extraordinary homicide is reported from a section of Williamsburg county, this state. M. W. Dennis, a white man, was conversing after supper with his wife, and they, after awhile, got to quarreling. Dennis, became greatly excited, and attempted to give his wife a genuine whipping. She remonstrated, but he continued his endeavor, and she then proceeded to defend herself. Happening to have in her lap a piece of iron, she used it in her own defense, striking him on his head and killing him instantly.
jerry-long-washington-1888-05-19.A6:
NEWS OF THE WEEK.
General Paine is to put the Volunteer in commission at once.

Kyrle Bellew has obtained an absolute divorce from his wife.

The Methodist Conference has decided to elect five new b shops.

Charles Francois Mangon, the distinguished French engineer is dead.

It is thought that the Government cable across Vineyard Sound has again parted.

The yacht Rambler will take sixty tons of dynamite to Aspinwall for the Panama Canal.

C. H. Reidel was convicted of murder in the first degree at Wilmington, Del., for the killing of his wife.

Four of the principal concert hall keepers in Cincinnati were arrested Sunday for violation of the new Sunday law.

A jury was obtained in the Kerr case, New York, Monday and District Attorney Fitzgerald opened for the people.

Harry Phillips, John L. Sullivan's manager, denies that he was connected with a burglary in Montreal, as charged.

Two students of Colby University, Waterville, Me., have varioloid. Precautions have been taken to prevent its spread.

The Bonapartists in the Chamber of Deputies, by combining with the Right, will try and bring about a dissolution of Parliament.

The Boston Herald, in furtherance of its profit-sharing agreement of over a year ago, divided $10,000 among its employees Saturday.

E. G. Walker, a colored lawyer, was Monday nominated by the Mayor of Boston as an assessor. No colored man has hitherto held that position.

John P. Webster, the oldest attorney in Somerset County, Me., was killed near his residence, in Norridgewock, Monday by falling from a railway bridge.

Miss Virginia W. Mason, the New York school teacher against whom charges of immorality have been made, vigorously denies the assertions against her.

A testimonial benefit was given in the Metropolitan Opera House Monday night to Lester Wallack, at which the best traged ans, actors and actresses took part.

A conference of the leaders of the Socialists was held Monday night at Chicago, to debate whether or not to put a Presidential ticket in the field. No decision was reached.

Angbury Bridgewater, the leader of a notorious band of guerillas during the war, and since then a lawless desperado, joined the Baptist Church at Moreland, Ky. Monday.

J. C Eversole was shot from ambush six weeks ago at Hazard, Ky. B. F. French and six others were indicted yesterday for the murder, which was the result of an old feud.

Rev. Edward J. Sourin, S. J., of St. Ignatius Catholic Church, died Sunday at Baltimore in the 80th year of his age. He was one of the best known priests in the country.

In the trial of Richard Kearney at Freehold, N. J., for the murder of Margaret Purcell, the jury yesterday returned a verdict of murder in the first degree after being out three hours.

A letter from Paris, received Saturday, was to the effect that Mr. Blaine had declined to say point blank whether he would or would not accept the Republican nomination for Presidency.

Tom Jones, a worthless character, at Dunlap, Ia., shot his wife in the head Thursday night, and then turned the revolver on himself, inflicting fatal wounds. The woman may recover.

Church people of all faiths in Chicago are protesting vigorously over the failure of the City Council to enact an ordinance prohibiting the location of saloons in the immediate vicinity of churches.

Word is received from Washington, Rhea County, Tenn., that the four colored men arrested Friday for assault on Mrs. Jane Whitney and an attempted assault on her daughter were lynched the same night.

Frank Durkin was found Saturday morning two miles from New Milford, Ct., lying under a tree near a quarry, where he worked, with his throat cut, reaching from ear to ear. He was waylaid. He may recover.

A SPECIAL from Spring City, Tenn., says: "Word has just reached here from Washington, the county seat of Rhea County, that four negro laborers on a new railroad, who were arrested for the assault of Mrs. Jane Whitney and an attempted brutal assault upon the person of her daughter, were taken from jail by an infuriated mob and lynched. joe-lotion-monticello-1888-08-14.A1:
Joe Lofton Captured.
Joe Lofton, the noted Lawrence county convict, was captured last Saturday. It seems that he was fired upon by a squad of men while standing in Wm. Russell's yard on Dry creek, and shot through the rump and elbow. He returned the fire, wounding Leon Branton, one of his assailants, in the thigh, and then took refuge in Russell's house, where he kept his assailants at bay until he could send for Sheriff Lee, to whom he surrendered. He was placed by the sheriff in the Monticello jail and kept there until Monday evening, when the sheriff, hearing that a mob was being organized to lynch Lofton, started with Geo. Garrett and Arthur Fox to carry his prisoner through the country to Jackson. Early Tuesday about 150 or 200 armed men rode into Monticello to lynch Lofton, and when they found the sheriff had spirited him away, their anger knew no bounds.

Later reports say Sheriff Lee's house was burned Tuesday night, his wife also being absent from home, and the presumption is that it was fired by some of the more extreme of the lynching party. It is also reported that the Sheriff will be petitioned to resign.
joe-lotion-monticello-1888-08-14.A2:
How Loftin was Captured.
Oakland, CA
How to get to Oakland, CA
Oakland, CA
Oakland,

There are so many erroneous reports about the arrest of Joseph E. Loftin, the escaped convict, that I concluded that I would make a true statement and ask you to publish it.

About ten months ago Loftin commenced to lie around my place and make threats that he intended to kill me and five others; also threatened that our wives should not bury us; that he intended to see that the buzzards should eat us. Some negroes that I had employed on my place saw Loftin get up out of a blind that he had made to shoot me out of. The whole settlement became terrorized by the threats and stealing that he was doing, or credited with doing. We stood this as long as we could, and our Sheriff, Mr. D. M. Lee, made no effort to arrest him. I then went to the Sheriff and got him to deputize me to arrest Loftin and he told me that he would render any assistance that I would need in the way of men or any thing else that I should need. With this assurance I commenced to hunt him with the assistance of A. M. Branton and three eighteen year old boys, and we hunted for him about three months and all the time we were hunting we could hear of his threats and stealing. On the 11th day of August, 1888, we found him at Will Russel's house on the Monticello and Columbia Ridge Road, ten and a half miles from Monticello. I sent Branton and two boys around on the backside of the house, while I and the other boy went up in front of the house. As we were going up the run of the branch in the direction of the house we scared up a drove of chickens that ran up to the house and that attracted the attention of Mrs. Russell and she came out of the house and looked around and went back, and then Mr. Russell came out and looked around and went back in a hurry. In about one minute Loftin came out with a gun in each hand and took advantage of some vines so that we could not see him any more until he got in about eighty yards of us. Then he had his gun leveled on the boy that was with me, and I fired on Loftin through some vines and broke his right arm. Then Loftin run a few steps and got behind a well curb and laid his gun on the curb and fired both barrels at us. One shot struck the boy three or four inches above the knee and went through his leg, and one cut through his hat and one shot cut my shirt on my left shoulder; one cut my shirt under my left arm and another my hat. Then I hollowed to him to lay down his arms and he told me to "shoot, God dam you." I tried to shoot him and my gum missed fire and I hollowed to Branton and his boys to close up and then Loftin ran in the direction of the house, but I could not see him until he got to the gate. As he went into the gate I fired on him again and he staggered and would have fallen but he caught to the gate for support. At this time the boy told me that he was shot, I looked at him and saw that he was bleeding so rapidly that he would have to have assistance. I then placed a sentinel there to see that Loftin could not be moved and went five miles to get a horse to carry off the boy, and before I could get the boy off and get back Loftin had sent after the Sheriff (who happened to be at church four and a half miles off) and he had got there and taken Loftin in a buggy and carried him to Monticello and put him in jail.
B. B. STRINGER.
joe-lotion-monticello-1888-08-14.A4:
The Recent Disturbances in Lawrence.
The recent occurrences in Lawrence county in connection with the noted convict Joe Loitin should not cause the people of that usually conservative and law-abiding county to be hastily or harshly judged. To any one acquainted with the history of the Loitin case, the action of the citizens of that county in at last becoming thoroughly aroused on the subject is most natural.

To begin with, Loitin murdered his elder brother in 1884, in a most brutal manner, and after being tried and sentenced to hang, his case was appealed and reversed by the Supreme Court on a technicality, a change of venue obtained to Coplah, and on the next trial he was convicted and sentenced to the Penitentiary for life—all at heavy cost to the Lawrence county tax-payers. He remained in the penitentiary but a short while, however, before he made his escape from the camps of the Gulf & Ship Island Railroad Co., and for more than a year has roamed at will his old haunts in Lawrence county, heavily armed and defying arrest. He boldly declared that Lawrence county owed himself and family a living and that he intended to have it, and at times went to the houses of persons, white and black, where he was not likely to meet with resistance, and demanded what he wanted. The lives of a number citizens who were witnesses against him or known to be unfriendly, were threatened, and they were in constant dread of being murdered from ambush, as he had murdered his brother. To add to the uneasiness of the situation, Loftin had a coterie of warm sympathizers and friends—just as the meanest criminals, no matter how bad, always have—and these helped to harbor him and it is believed, aided him in certain acts of lawlessness, thus furnishing a constant menace to the peace and quiet of the community. Some time ago one man's barn was fired in the night, and when he rushed out to extinguish the flames, he was filled with buck-shot.

So far as is known, the Penitentiary Lessees, though apprised of Loftin's whereabouts, made no effort to recapture him, and it is said the Sheriff of the county, though acquainted with the facts, and though Loftin actually visited Monticello during the late term of Court, was likewise indifferent, and made no effort whatever to capture him until after Loftin's movements led to the killing of Sauls a few weeks ago, and then not until he had been earnestly importuned to do so.

It was no wonder, therefore, that the best citizens of the county should have finally become thoroughly exasperated and resolved on visiting summary justice upon Loftin when he was captured. At the same time we think the sheriff should not be censured for doing what he could to protect Loftin after he was caught. It is a sheriff's sworn duty to faithfully protect a prisoner in his custody, and in doing this, Sheriff Lee was but following in the line of his official duty. What he should be blamed for is what he failed to do before being sent for by Loftin.

As to the burning of the Sheriff's house, that cannot be justified or condoned on any ground, and we feel warranted in saying it is not looked upon with the least allowance by the great mass of the people of the county, without regard to their opinion of the sheriff's course in reference to Loftin.

On the whole, it is to be hoped that what has occurred will serve as an effectual warning to criminals and lax officials in our sister county, and that the one will be deterred from further acts of lawlessness and the other to be more zealous in the discharge of all their official duties. And first in the latter's line of duty will come a diligent effort to apprehend and convict the sneak who burned the sheriff's house.

P. S.—After the above was put in type we received the letter from Mr. B. B. Stringer which is published in another column, giving some interesting particulars as to how the capture of Loftin was brought about.
joe-lotion-monticello-1888-08-14.A6:
LAWRENCE AROUSED.
The Indignant Citizens Hold a Meeting, Recite Their Grievances in the Joe Loftin Matter and Ask Their Sheriff to Resign.
Also a Wholesome Warning to Loftin's Pals and Sympa- thizers.
The following resolutions were adopted by a citizen's meeting held in Monticello, Tuesday, Aug 14th, and speak for themselves:

WHEREAS, We, the citizens of Lawrence county, having found out that it was not Joseph E. Loftin alone that has given us all the trouble that we have undergone for the past 12 or 13 months, but men claiming the title of citizens have harbored and even assisted him, either directly or indirectly, in perpetrating his inhuman and heinous acts, and now that we have found out by diligent search and inquiry each and every one, both male and female, white and colored, that is, or have been heretofore participants in this lawlessness, we, as citizens, advise them to act in the future as good citizens, or suffer the consequences; and

WHEREAS, We feel very much aggrieved at the conduct of our Sheriff, D. M. Lee, for lying neutral for 12 months, being almost daily informed of J. E. Loftin's whereabouts, taking no steps to arrest said J. E. Loftin until some of our distressed citizens pressed their services on him to hunt down and arrest said fugitive when he then privately deputized one B. B. Stringer to arrest said Loftin, who wounded him in the combat so that he could not have possibly escaped, and was left under guard of one of Stringer's men until he could recruit his force and attend to one of his men, who was also shot in the combat. In the meantime, Loftin sent after our Sheriff, D. M. Lee, to come and protect him—who disarmed private citizens at the request of Loftin before he would allow them to enter the house where Loftin lay, allowing Joe Loftin to retain his weapons, which consisted of two shot guns, one six shooter and one dirk knife. And we believe an injustice has been wrought by the action of the Sheriff in this matter, as Loftin should have been hanged higher than Haman, which sentence was pronounced by Judge Mayers; therefore be it
Resolved, That we, the citizens of Lawrence county, ask D. M. Lee to resign his office of Sheriff.
Be it further Resolved, That all the citizens of Lawrence county be requested to meet in Monticello, on the 25th day of August, 1888, at 11 o'clock, a. m.
Resolved, That a copy of these resolutions be published in the Lawrence County Press.
joe-lotion-monticello-1888-08-14.A7:
Statement from Sheriff Lee of Lawrence County.
On arriving at Silver Creek church, August 11th, 1888, I was informed that Joseph E. Loftin was at A. W. W. Russell's wounded and wanted me to go to him. I was also informed that he had two guns and a pistol. Mr. Webb Langston and I hastened to where he was. When we arrived at the gate, I sent Mr. Langston to tell Loftin I was there and wanted to come in where he was. After several minutes, Mr. Langston returned and stated that Loftin said to "come in, but not attempt to arrest him." I immediately went in, and as I entered the door I spoke to him. He, with pistol in hand, said, "Don't try to arrest me, for I don't want to shoot you." I saw he was considerably excited and knew he would shoot while in that state of mind, so I thought the easiest way was the best, and I began to talk and coax him to surrender. He asked me if I would disarm him, put him in jail and send him back to the Penitentiary. I told him plainly I would. He replied, "I hate to go there; don't bother me yet, but stay awhile." I plainly saw he was yielding, and that I could presently disarm him without any violent means. By this time, several gentlemen had come. Among the rest, Mr. Charles Ellzey. Loftin seemed to be afraid of Mr. Ellzey, and again became excited. To assure him that no one meant to harm him, I asked and slightly searched Mr. Ellzey, not that I cared for his being armed, but in order to get Loftin's arms before anything rash was done.

I am sure Mr. Ellzey is a reasonable man and can understand this, and will denounce some of the rash acts that have been committed against me. As to disarming private citizens, there is no truth in it.

When I got ready to start, I took Loftin's guns, gave one to R. A. Daniels and the other to Dr. Larkin, and made him give me his pistol, which I belted around myself, and come to Monticello and placed Loftin in jail. Up to this time, I did not know who shot Loftin, neither had I seen or heard of Stringer's guard. He was in jail two days and I was reliably informed that he would be mobbed. I cared nothing about Loftin, and would have been glad could he have been put out of the way, neither do I censure any man for trying to mob him, but it is a dreadful thing to hold a prisoner for an infuriated mob, thus becoming officially, legally and morally responsible for his life. So I run him off and placed him in the Penitentiary.

I returned to Monticello to find myself homeless, but not friendless. "Tis true, I occasionally heard of Loftin's being in the county, and when I found out his confederates and route, I secretly went to laying plans to trap him. It is not necessary to state what plans, for all intelligent men know such things must necessarily be secret.

Finally, I deputized B. B. Stringer and R. D. Fugler, as they thought they could get him, and wanted the reward. In the meantime, we talked over the matter and decided a still hunt would be best. And when Mr. Stringer shot Loftin, I suppose there must have been at least fifty men who knew it before I did, for I was late in getting to church and then was the time for them to have taken him, but on the contrary, no one wanted to go with me to where he was.

Before I resign I would be glad that the men who participated in that meeting would sign their names to the article asking me to resign, so I would know how many live in Lawrence, Lincoln, Pike and Marion counties. At least I think the Chairman and Secretary's names should have been attached to the resolutions.

I see in the Press that the so-called citizens' of Lawrence county adjourned to meet on the 25th inst. This proposed meeting is uncalled for and illegal, and I, as Sheriff of Lawrence county, respectfully and politely request all good citizens not to attend said meeting, and I shall take some legal steps to disband the other class. Such meetings have a demoralizing tendency and drive men to desperation. If this state of affairs continues instead of having one man in the woods you will have one dozen. Then you must remember that in attending these meetings you are backing up a bad element and thus encourage them to do their heinous deeds and thereby you become accessory to their crimes.

Respectfully submitted,
D. M. LEE,

A dispatch from Port Gibson says:
joe-lotion-monticello-1888-08-14.A8: We publish in another column an interesting statement from Sheriff Lee, of Lawrence county, in regard to the Loftin matter. This statement, together with the endorsement of the large mass meeting on last Wednesday, places Mr. Lee in good shape throughout the Loftin affair—a fact we note with pleasure.
joe-lotion-monticello-1888-08-14.A9:
LAWRENCE COUNTY.
A LARGE CITIZENS' MEETING DEPRECATES THE ACTION OF CITIZENS' MEETING NO 1, ENDORSES THE COURSE OF SHERIFF LEE,
And Pledges That the Law Shall Reign Supreme.
Morganism, Aug. 29, 1888.
Monticello, Aug. 22, 1888.

At a mass meeting of the citizens of Lawrence county this day, on motion J. J. Denson was elected temporary chairman and J. A. Rowan Secretary.

On motion of C. R. Dale the temporary organization was made permanent.

On motion, a committee of five, one from each supervisor's district, was appointed to select a vice-president from each district, and two assistant secretaries to complete the organization. Committee—Beat 1, T. H. Smith; Beat 2, C. O. Nelson; Beat 3, H. H. Smith; Beat 4, A. Fairly; Beat 5, W. R. Bourne.

Said committee reported the following names as vice-presidents, to-wit: Beat 1, H. I. Bird; Beat 2, J. B. Smith; Beat 3, O. F. Wilson; Beat 4, J. H. Williams; Beat 5, W. J. Patterson; assistant secretaries, J. E. Thomas, I. M. C. Smith.

The following resolution was offered by J. W. Welborn and adopted:

Resolved, That those who participated in the meeting of the 14th inst., and who feel that they were wrong and who now recant, be invited to take part in this meeting, and that they be accepted as acting now in good faith.

On motion a committee of five, one from each Supervisor's district, was appointed on resolutions, as follows: Beat 1, T. H. Smith; Beat 2, C. O. Nelson; Beat 3, J. C. Lambert; Beat 4, A. T. Longino; Beat 5, W. R. Bourne.

On motion the presiding officers and secretaries were added to the committee, who offered the following resolutions:

WHEREAS, There appeared in the Lawrence County Press of August 16th, 1888, proceedings of a mass meeting purporting to be from the law-abiding citizens of Lawrence county, in which a resolution appears requesting the sheriff, D. A family feud between Captain Richard Hagan and the Huffmans, of Blythewood, Fairfield county, South Carolina, terminated recently in the cowardly assassination of the former. Capt. Hogan was one of the most distinguished scouts in Gen. Lee's army and was aver fifty years of age. The Huffmans are a numerous family, there being six sons and the father. Tom Huffman and Capt. They remained engaged for two years, and during that time her lover accomplished her ruin, and just before the matter was brought before Capt. Hogan's attention he fled the country. The outraged father pursued his daughter's deceiver for three months, and traveled over four thousand miles, but nothing has ever been heard of Tom Huffman. The poor girl could not survive her disgrace. Last spring it came to Capt. Hogan's ears that the other Huffman brothers were talking in an insulting way about his other daughter. He at once procured a horsehip and publicly cowhidled Charlie and Butler Huffman. The Huffmans armed and were going to attack him when they were all arested and put under a peace bond. One of them could not give bond and fled the country, but two weeks ago he returned to his home and has been concealed there. The other night Capt. Hogan was walking from the post-office to his house and was holding the hand of his 9-year-old son. When within fifty yards of his residence two men sprang into the road behind him and shot him in the back. They then fled. Captain Hogan fell, but he drew his pistol and fired at the retreating figures without effect. Charles and Jack Huffman were arrested the next morning and committed to jail, and all the others were put under bond to appear on trial. A NEBRASKA LYNCHING.
The Author of a Shocking Crime Sum- marily Dealt With.
Webster county, Nebraska, in which two weeks ago the lynching of the desperado Bill Cole took place, was Sept. 1 the scene of a similar event. This second outbreak of lawless justice was the sequel of one of the most horrible tragedies in the history of crime. It occurred on a farm belonging to a man named Weeks, living not far from Gulde Rock. He was having his threshing done, and among those in his employ was a man named John Baker. Baker was feeding the thresher and had a young boy cutting bands for him. While the men were thus engaged the boy, in cutting a band, accidentally let the knife slip, striking Baker on the hand and inflicting an ugly wound. Wild with rage, Baker, dropping a bundle which he had in his hand, reached for the boy. The latter attempted to escape but before he could do so the infuriated man had him in his grasp and lifting him bodily into the air, threw him on the platform. In a moment the boy's feet were among the cruel teeth of the thresher and Baker was crowding him in as if he were a sheaf of grain. The boy screamed for help, but it is evident that several moments elapsed before the other men at work about the thresher distinguished his voice about the roar, for when they rushed to the front of the machine half of his body had already disappeared and Baker was still holding the quivering remains. On seeing the other men Baker released his hold an jumping from the platform attempted to escape. In a moment however, the men were upon him and he was a prisoner. The boy was dead and only the upper portion of his body remained. The platform of the thresher was covered with blood, the teeth of the machine were dyed with it, and bits of clothing, bone and flesh were brought to view with every revolution. 'Hang him!' shouted one of the men, and in an instant a stout rope was about Baker's neck and he was dragged struggling to the rear of the machine. One of the men quickly ascended and climbing out on the straw carrier took one end of the rope passed it through one of the iron rods. As soon as the rope came within reaching distance of the ground a half dozen strong hands had hold of it. Baker's arms were pinioned behind him and in less time than it takes to tell it he was swung between earth and sky while the platform of the thresher was still warm with his victim's blood.

St. HELENA, April 22.—A shooting affair occurred here at 2 o'clock this morning which will doubtless result in the death of a young man named Budd Vann. He with some companions were standing near a house of ill-fame, when one of the crowd threw a rock though a window of the house, striking one of the inmates. Graham, a brother of one of the women of the house, was inside at the time and picking up a revolver fired into the crowd, hitting young Vann in the abdomen, inflicting a fatal wound. He was immediately arrested. The injured man is thought to be dying. There is great excitement over the shooting.

ST. HELENA, Cal., May 5.—John Wright, who shot and killed Budd Vann in this town two weeks ago, was taken from jail early this morning by a mob of masked men and hanged to the bridge at the head of Main street. Wright had been confined in the county jail at Napa since the shooting, but was brought here yesterday for his preliminary examination. No one suspected that an attempt at lynching would be made. At 1 o'clock this morning Justice Elgin, who had the jail keys, was called to his door, surrounded by a mob and forced to give up the keys. The crowd then took the prisoner from the jail, and in ten minutes his body was hanging from the bridge. No arrests have been made, but the tragedy is deplored by law-abiding citizens. The shooting of young Vann occurred near a house of ill-fame. Vann and some companions were standing near by, when some one threw a rock at a window. Wright, who was a brother of the inmate, was in the house at the time, and immediately fired a pistol, the shot striking Vann.

The streets have been thronged all day with people discussing this mornings tragedy. The body of the deceased, left by the lynchers swinging from the bridge, remained and was viewed by the passers by until about eight this morning, when an undertaker cut it down by order of the Sheriff, and the Coroner was landed on the ground, trying to get some evidence of the perpetrators of the outrage. At the coroner's inquest this afternoon no new facts were brought out and there was no clue obtainable. The jury brought in a verdict to the effect that Wright came to his death by violence at the hands of unknown persons, and they severely censured the police officers of the town for gross neglect of duty in leaving the jail unguarded.

The pastors of the various Baptist churches in the State held memorial services last Sunday morning in honor of the life, character and work of the late Mat thew Tyson Yates, D. D., a native of this State, who resided in Shanghai, China, for 41 years, as the Senior Missionary of the Southern Baptist Convention. Rev. H. A. Brown, the efficient pastor of the Baptist Church here, preached a sermon in honor of the beloved Divine Sunday morning, and his effort was both appropriate and interesting. The Roanoke & Southern Railroad.

During the past week surveyors of the R. & S. road have been busy locating the line around the city, and everything seems to be moving along in a rapid and satisfactory manner. Fourteen miles of the road from Martinsville, Va., to the North Carolina line have been let to Messrs. Breen & Feely, contractors, of Alexandria, Va., work upon which will commence at once. As soon as the surveying is completed the directors state that work will commence at the Winston end. Hands are to be placed all along the line, as the contractors have made arrangements to commence grading at Madison, Rockingham county, and have already rented a factory at that place to be used for a stockade. It is said that the road will run directly by three mica mines, a tin mine, an iron mine, and over a rich coal field in the short distance between Ridgeway and Madison.

Let the good work move forward!

Orchestra Concerts.

The Salem Orchestra repeated their concert in the Academy Chapel last Thursday night. It was given complimentary to the young ladies of the Academy, though a number of other friends were in attendance, all of whom enjoyed the entertainment very much. The concert of Thursday night surpassed any previous effort made by the Orchestra. The program throughout was entertaining, and each one present will join us in returning thanks to each member for the evening so pleasantly spent.

The Orchestra will give a concert at the Opera House to-morrow (Friday) night for the benefit of the Twin-City Hospital. Both the Orchestra and the cause for which the concert will be given merit a liberal patronage from our citizens. Prof. W. A. Blair has consented to deliver an address, and those who attend the concert may hear something good. Go out to hear them and carry your sister. If you haven't any sister carry somebody else's.

The Railroad Meeting at Danbury.

A meeting was held at Danbury last Wednesday to see if the people of Stokes county were in favor of voting a subscription to the Roanoke & Southern Railroad, which is to be built from Winston to Roanoke City, Va. We are informed that much enthusiasm was manifested in the meeting, and that speeches were made by representatives from Winston and from several parts of Stokes county, all of whom favored the proposition to vote a subscription to the road should it be built centrally through Stokes county. It seems that it would cost more to run the road through Danbury than it would to locate it on any other route, and in order to secure the road through that place the county of Stokes would necessarily have to vote a liberal subscription. Some think the county would be justified in voting all that may be asked, in order to secure the road. We learn that an election will be called shortly for the citizens of Stokes to decide the matter. THE SENTINEL trusts that the people will act wisely by voting for the subscription, which will benefit them and their county beyond estimate.

Killed a Roustabout.
Lee Andrew Huff, first mate of the steamer Coahoma, shot and killed an unknown colored rouster while the boat was lying at Concordia, Miss., 215 miles south of this city, about 6 o'clock Saturday morning.

Walter Jackson, colored, an eye witness to the affair, was seen by an Appeal reporter and made the following statement: "Early Saturday morning the boat landed at Concordia to take on some freight. Among the rousters employed on the boat to handle freight was a colored man somewhat slower than the others. The mate frequently quarreled with him and on two occasions thrashed him. Just before the killing the mate ordered the man to go ashore and bring aboard some cotton seed. The latter obeyed but was very slow. This seemed to anger the mate who knocked him down and beat him up very badly. Realizing that he would be killed unless he made his escape the negro ran off the boat followed by Huff. At the end of the stage plank Huff struck at the negro with a stick, but missed. He then pulled his pistol and fired three shots, the bullets taking effect, one in the head, one in the left hip and the other in the back. The wounded man lived only a few minutes. Huff escaped.

Negro Killed by a Steamboat Mate.
MEMPHIS, Tenn.. July 29. — Yesterday, at Concordia, Miss., a difficulty occurred between Lee Huff, mate of the steamer Coahoma, and one of the colored deck crew, which resulted in the killing of the negro, who, while attempting to cut the mate, was shot three times. The shooting created great excitement, and fearing violence at the hands of the negroes, who are largely in the majority at Concordia, the mate was rowed across the river to the Arkansas side, and will doubtless join his boat here.
leander-huff-concordia-landing-1888-07-2.A4:
A BACE FOR LIFE.
Hunted by a Crowd of Vengeance- Seeking Negroes
A Memphis (Tenn.) special says: While the steamer Coahoma was loading cottonseed at Concordia Landing, Miss., 180 miles below Memphis, early yesterday morning one of the negro rostabouts, who was not working to suit the mate, Leander Huff, was ordered to "move lively," and for answer drew a knife and struck the mate. The point of the blade caught Huff's sleeve and ripped it from the cuff to the elbow. Huff instantly drew his pistol, and the rouster turned. Huff pulled the trigger, firing three shots in rapid succession. The negro ran 100 yards and fell dead, with one ball in his neck, one in his shoulder, and one in his side. About twenty negroes who had been lottering about the landing demanded that Huff be given up to them, threatening to burn the boat if he was not handed over to be swung up. There was no time to raise the gang-plank and back out, but Huff succeeded in getting into a yawl on the other side of the steamer, one of the crew rowing him across to an island near the Arkansas shore.

The Coahoma steered across after it, intending to fake Huff on board, but a skiff-load of excited negroes landed about the same time and Huff seeing them started off down the island. Other skiffs filled with negroes were seen going toward the island as the steamer moved away. It is doubtful if Huff escaped, but he is a good swimmer and if he got to the Arkansas bank of the island he may have succeeded in getting away into the brush. The country is wild, sparsely settled, and without telegraphic communication. The steamer returned to Memphis to-night, but no additional particulars could be learned.
