ESCAPED FROM THE MOB. Terrible Experience of a Man Pur-sued By Blood-Thirsty Negroes.
Memphis, Aug. 3.—(Special.)—Leander Huff, the mate of the steamer Coahoma, who was believed to have been lynched on the island opposite Carson's Landing' five days ago, has turned up alive, and relates a thrilling story of his escape and sufferings. The mob of negroes which forced him to fly for his life, after he had killed the roustabout at Carson's Landing, pursued him so closely that he was afraid to attempt to cross the island, after having reached it; but after dodging about half an hour or more, he hid himself in the young cane in the edge of a brake, lying at full length upon the ground. Two or three negroes crossed over from Carson's to the Island, and made a systematic search. A score of times he narrowly escaped discovery. He lay in that position all night, and at 4 o'clock in the morning started for the Arkansas side of the Island. Tying his pistol, money and clothes in a bundle, and strapping it to the back of his neck, he swam half a mile across a chute to the Arkansas shore. It was not until sundown of that day that he succeeded in getting anything to eat. He procured a scant meal from a fisherman, whom he found in his boat tied up to the bank. The fisherman did not know who he was, but told him the woods were full of negroes. hunting for Huff. He did not reveal his identity, but pushed on, traveling day and night up the river bank through swamps, and swimming bayous, until he heard the welcome whistle of the Coahoma on her return trip from Memphis. He was in a fearful plight when he was taken aboard. His clothing hung in shreds, his feet and hands were swollen to twice their usual size, and every inch of his skin inflamed by poison oak. He was brought to Memphis yesterday and taken in a closed hack to the house of a friend, where he remained concealed until last night, when a purse of $200 was made up for him by the officers of the boat and a ticket purchased for him to some Eastern point. He says he will not return to Carson's now, as he knows his life would not be safe, but will go there in the fall and stand his trial.
leander-huff-concordia-landing-1888-07-2.A14:
HUFF'S TERRIBLE EXPERIENCE. Days and Nights in a Swamp, Hunted by Negroes Bent Upon Killing Him. From the St. Louis Republic.
MEMPHIS, Tenn., Aug. 3.—Leander Huff, the mate of the steamer Cochoma, arrived here to-day after a terrible experience as a fugitive on the river below. Last Saturday night, while the boat was lying at Concordia Landing, 160 miles from Memphis. Huff shot and killed a negro deckhand who was making at him with a knife. A crowd of negroes on the bank immediately made a rush for the boat, yelling "Kill him," and before the gangplank could be raised half a score of them were upon it.

Huff ran to the after guard of the boat and lowered a skiff. The mob was so close on him that he had barely time to jump into the frail craft and push off when the foremost of them struck at him with a hatchet and clipped a piece out of his left ear. Seeing that their prey was about to escape, the negroes ran ashore and got skiffs and put out after him. It was a race for life, and with a single car he contrived to reach a low, swampy island, two miles down the river, before his pursuers could overtake him. They fired a number of shots at him, but without effect.

Abandoning the boat he fled into the jungle, closely followed by the howling mob. He had gone but a short distance when his feet were caught by a vine and he fell headlong into the mire. The accident saved him, for the tall marsh grass covered him, and the nature of the ground prevented the leaving of a trail. Several times the mob passed so close he could have touched them with his hand, but after a brief search they left, doubtless thinking that he had gone to the river bank, a short distance further on.

All that day and night and all the next day he lay in his hiding place, tormented by mosquitoes and in deadly fear of the moccasins that he could see in the grass. He could hear the voices of the negroes from time to time, and was afraid to stir. At last they passed him on their return to the landing place, and he knew from what they said that they were satisfied that he had left the island.

When darkness came he crept down to the river bank and plunged in to swim to the Arkansas shore, half a mile distant. He reached the bank more dead than alive, and dragged himself along the levee all night, hoping to catch a boat. At daylight he reached the hut of a white fisherman, who gave him the first food he had tasted in three days. The fisherman's boat was gone to a point fifty miles below, which cut off any chance of escape in that quarter. He told the fugitive that the levee above and below was patrolled for miles by armed negroes on the lookout for him.

Again Huff turned and plunged into the swamps. Weak and weary as he was, he was compelled to swim two lakes in order to make the wide circuit that would enable him to elude the dusky watchers. About 5 o'clock the following afternoon he again reached the river. But no sooner had he mounted the levee than ten or fifteen negroes made their appearance and ran toward him with exultant shouts.

"Better drown than be killed by these black devils," was Huff's despairing thought. Gathering his little remaining strength for the effort, he ran down the bank and leaped into the stream, diving as far as possible to escape the bullets that he knew would be sent after him. How he managed to escape drowning is a mystery. "I was past swimming," said Huff, in relating his experience to-day. "and I do not remember anything that passed. The first thing I knew a log floated by me, and I crawled upon it. Some time during the night I hailed a passing boat, and was taken on board. Then I fainted away, and knew no more until a cabin boy waked me and said Memphis was in sight."
leander-huff-concordia-landing-1888-07-2.A15:
A MURDERER CAPTURED.
LEE HUFF ARRESTED FOR KILLING A NEGRO ON THE KATE ADAMS.
He Swims the Mississippi to Escape the Fury of a Mob of Negroes Keeping the Crowd at Bay With a Pistol.
Lee Andrew Huff, the steamboat mate who shot and killed a negro roustabout aboard the steamer Kate Adams in Coahoma County, Miss., last summer, was captured yesterday afternoon by Patrolman Mahon, in Brown's saloon, corner Main and Washington streets. Huff was taken to the station-house and locked up on a charge of being a fugitive from justice.

Since the killing Huff has been going under the name of Charles Howard. He was seen in his cell by an Appeal reporter and made a full statement about the affair, also gave the names of the places he has visited since the trouble. He said that on the morning of the killing he ordered the negro, who was a lazy and stupid fellow, to be more active or he would discharge him. The negro made an insolent reply and went to the rear of boat. Shortly afterward he came for again and began cursing Huff, also ened to whip him. Huff became and picked up a stick, with which he h. the negro on the head, knocking him. In an instant the rouster was upon feet again, and with a large knife in hand, attacked the mate. Hum retreated a few steps, pulled a pistol and warned the fellow that if he advanced another step it would be at the peril of his life. The negro did not heed the warning and made a rush for the steps, whereupon the mate fired, the bullet entering the negro's breast near the heart. Death was almost instantaneous. The report of the pistol was heard all over the boat, and in less time than it takes to tell it, the bow of the boat was crowded with negroes. When they learned the cause of the shooting they became very demonstrative, and threatened to hang the mate and burn the boat. The crowd was finally dispersed and the steamer continued on her voyage up the river. When the next landing was reached Huff got off and was followed by several negroes. When the boat was well out of sight the negroes, about twelve in number, advanced towards the mate in a threatening manner. To save his life he jumped into the river and swam to the opposite shore, Island Seventy-one, which he reached in safety, though almost exhausted. The negroes followed in skiffs, but were kept from landing by Huff, who pulled a pistol and swore that the first one who came ashore would be killed. This had the desired effect and the negroes made no further effort to land. Huff remained on the island until the next morning, when a party of whites rescued him and conducted him to a place of safety. He staid with his rescuers until a passing steamer took him aboard and brought him to this city. When the boat touched the wharf he got off and boarded a train for Cairo, where he remained several weeks. Leaving there he went to St. Louis, thence to Chicago and finally came South again, stopping first at a station in Arkansas, where he remained several weeks, after which he came to Memphis and has been here ever since. Huff says he is confident he will be acquitted and will return to Mississippi without a requisition.

The Journal of the House.

WASHINGTON, April 13.—The clerk proceeded to read the journal of the legislative day, Wednesday, April 4. The journal consists of ninety manuscript pages, exclusive of seventy-one rolls. Mr. Dockery, of Missouri, asked unanimous consent to dispense with the reading, but Mr. E.B. Taylor and Mr. Grosvenor interposed objection. They did not, however, demand the reading of the roll calls in full, as such reading would occupy two or three days. The reading occupied exactly one hour.

Washington Lady Commits Suicide.

WASHINGTON, April 13.—Mrs. Bulkeley committed suicide last night by taking poison. She was the only daughter of Judge Curtis J. Hillier, and eloped with young Bulkeley some months ago. She separated from him after marriage. A few days afterwards she went to live with him, and after a short time returned to her parents. It is supposed that she was suffering from temporary insanity.

Of Course There was no Trace.

ATTICA, N. Y., April 13.—The First National bank, St. Johnsville, was robbed between 12 and 3 this morning. Entrance was gained through a back window. Less than $10,000 in cash and $820 in unsigne bills, a gold watch and chain valued at $175, together with other jewelry left for safe-keeping, were taken. There is no trace of the burglars.

Attempted Abduction.

LOUISVILLE, April 13.—Lee McElroy, a colored youth 15 years of age, this morning stole a three-year-old child, Robert Hoskins, white. The little one was playing in the front yard. The negro boy was found hiding with the child in a corner lot near his home. He said he intended to hold the child for ransom.

A "Q" engineer in Chicago who was stoned by a crowd at Forty seventh street fired in return, wounding one man in the knee. At Fortieth street another crowd pelted him and he fired again, wounding a Wabash engineer fatally. He was arrested.

It is stated that Prince Bismarck has abandoned his opposition to the marriage of Prince Alexander of Battenburg and Princess Victoria, having gained certain other concessions, and that all the differences between the Emperor and Prince Bismarck are now settled.

Lee McElroy, a colored youth aged 15 years, stole a three-year old child of Robert Haskins, a business man of Louisville, Ky. A search found the negro hiding with the child, which he said he intended to hold for a ransom. His age saved him from a lynching.

The Cologne Gazette says Prince Bismarck has brought the question of the marriage of Prince Alexander and Princess Victoria to a standstill. It is stated that in November last Bismarck declared to the Czar that such a marriage should never take place, at least while his advice was accepted.

The St. Paul Pioneer Press learns from Billings, Montana, of the capture of two notorious criminals having in their possession fifty-eight head of horses bearing tenteen well-known Nevada brands. One man has been recognized as Teton, a noted horse thief and murderer, for whose capitals there are rewards aggregating $6,000 in Idaho and Nevada.

At the village of Savoy in Texas, there occurred a few days ago a wedding which was remarkable for the age and prominence of the groom. The contracting parties were Major Sivils, of Grayson county, aged 82, and a well-to-do widow, aged 50. Major Sivils served through the Mexican and civil wars. According to a New York dispatch there was a great deal of mystery connected with the funeral of Jacob Sharp. The utmost secrecy marked the arrangements, and no one was allowed to enter the house except by invitation especially sent by the family. Even visitors had evidently been instructed not to give any information about the affair, and when questioned denied that the funeral was taking place. The question is being debated as to whether or not he is really dead.

The Pope Leo has sent a letter to President Cleveland thanking him for the jubilee present of a copy of the constitution. The communication was handed to the President by Cardinal Gibbons. The Pope speaks of the great distinction of receiving from the ruler of a free people a gift which he had never expected to be sent him, and expresses his appreciation of the present. The Pope wishes peace and prosperity, and prays for the American people and the country perpetuation of their institutions, liberty and a plentitude of God's favor.

The English undoubtedly admire Mr. Cleveland, but not because he is in favor of free trade, for, as a rule, people over there know little and care little whether a man is a Democrat or a Republican.

The report of the public printer, Benedict, for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1887, has been submitted to congress. It claims that the public printer has added greatly to the convenience and working capacity of the office, but still there are marked deficiencies that ought to be supplied. The output of public printing for the year was considerably larger than ever before, and this result, which has disposed of a great deal of delayed work, was accomplished at a cost greatly below the average of the previous years. The report claims that the actual cost was $262,481 less than the cost of the preceding year.

Tolsma, a citizen of that state, alleging that his nets have been seized and that he has been unlawfully deprived by the Canadian authorities of the right to fish in St. Mary's river. The value of the exports of breadstuffs for the twelve months ended December 31, 1887, was $158,301,768, as against $146,123,020 for the twelve months ended December 31, 1886.

The house has received the annual report of the board of managers of the national homes for disabled volunteer soldiers. The average number of inmates present during the year was 9,718, an increase of forty-four per cent, during the last five years. The death rate for the year was sixty-one per cent, more than the rate of men of similar ages in ordinary health. During the past three years the number of those admitted on account of wounds received during action has materially fallen off, while those received owing to age infirmatives greatly increased. and specifications shall be submitted to and approved by the secretary of war before the work is begun.

LEWIS DAVIS LYNCHED.
Brutal Work of a Mob in Crawford County, Mo. CURA Mo. Sept. 24 - Lewis Davis
CUBA, Mo., Sept. 24.—Lewis Davis, who for six months has been confined in the St. Louis jail on the charge of murdering his neighbor and friend, David Miller, and who was brought here last Tuesday for trial at the Circuit Court now in session, was taken from jail and hung by a mob. Masked men came into town about two o'clock this morning, battered down the iron doors of the jail, led him away and lynched him.

HIS CRIME.

Davis was charged with the murder of David Miller on the 2d of last January. On that day Miller left home to meet Davis and go to town twelve miles off, to pay his taxes. He never returned and, after a week's search, was found murdered, shot through the head and his pockets rifled. The bullet found in his brain fitted the pistol found on Davis, which had a peculiar rifle in the bore. There were other circumstances that pointed to Davis' guilt including proven falsehoods told by Davis as to his whereabouts. He would have been mobbed at the time he was arrested, but was taken to St. Louis for safe-keeping. A jury had been selected to try him and the case would have been called at 11 o'clock to-morrow.

THE LYNCHING.

This morning, between 2 and 3 o'clock, a runner came to the Sheriff and informed him that there was a mob coming, and he sent R. P. Dunlap, deputy sheriff, to inform Judge Bland, who was stopping at the hotel, and got some advice as to what to do; but the deputy only got a short distance when he met the mob, about forty masked men, who took him in charge and marched him back to the jail. They then went to a blacksmith shop and procured coal chisels and hammers and returned to the jail and cut the door down.

Only one guard was on duty at the jail and he was soon mastered. Davis fought desperately with a piece of the heavy bedstead in his cell, but was overpowered and led away with a rope around his neck. Every street was guarded; no one was allowed to witness the tragedy.

They put a rope around Davis' neck and forced him out and took him about a half mile north of Steelville, on the Cuba road, and hung him to the limb of a post oak tree, immediately over the grave of Pat Wallace, who was hung by a mob October 4, 1886, for the murder of the Logan family.

Circum Court was in session last week and will meet next week. Davis' case would have come up for trial Monday. The jury was already selected and was composed of the best men in Crawford County, and there is no doubt that Davis would have been convicted of murder in the first degree. No doubt the mob was enraged by the acquittal of Elbert Clonts, who was tried here last week under an indictment for the murder of his father some three years ago.

WILL BE INVESTIGATED.

The better class of society of this county discourage mobs and mob violence, and are very anxious that the guilty parties be brought to justice. There is strong suspicion that the leaders of this mob are some of the same parties that lynched Pat Wallace two years ago, and the matter will be investigated, as Judge Bland has ordered a special grand jury composed of the representative men of the county to inquire into the matter, and says all violators of the law must be punished to the full extent of the law.

The light brightening—that is, the fog growing more luminous, without appearing to thin—the boat's outline lay visible, together with her furniture, such as the sail and the oars. I tenderly laid Imogene's cold hand down, and turning the sail over found—as I had expected—the mast lying under it; and, partly peering and partly groping, I made out an iron clamp fitted to the foremost thwart or seat, with a hollow under it in the bottom of the boat for receiving the heel of the mast.

I lifted the spar and very easily stepped it, discovering that the halliards for hoisting the sail were ready rove through a small block seized to the head of the mast. I hauled upon this rope to clear the sail, and perceived it to be shaped like a lug, fitted to a pard, only the yard was arched, causing the head of the sail to appear like a bow when the arrow is drawn upon it. Before setting the sail I went aft, and by dint of feeling and staring discovered a rope grummet or hempen hook fastened to the larboard horn, but close in, so that it lay out of sight against the boat's stern. 'Twas very clear that this was meant to receive an oar for steering, but whether or not it would serve my turn for that purpose. So, without more ado I rove an earth through the grummet, then hoisted the sail, making the tack fast to the larboard horn on the bow, and came aft with the sheet.

The boat instantly felt the pressure, and the wind being abaft the beam she slipped along like a sledge, as you will suppose, when I say that her bottom was shaped like the side of a pea shell, and that her whole frame might have been imitated from one of those black pods of seaweed which are furnished by nature with wire-like projections, and which may be found in plenty upon our seacoast. The oar controlled her very capitally.

The double motive I had for getting away from this place—dest, to run out of the fog and so get light to enable me to minister to Imogene, and next to remove myself so far from the Death Ship as to render pursuit hopeless even should the thickness in the bay clear up and enable Vanderdecken to recover his boat which I had cut adrift; this double motive. I say, lifted my anxiety and eagerness to the height of madness. My dearest lay with her head toward me, and in the glistening white obscurity I could discern her pale face upon the pillow of my coat, but could not tell whether her eyes were open or shut. She did not moan: she lay as still as the dead. I asked her if she was in pain. She said no, but in a voice so feeble that I had to bend my ear to catch the syllable.

I could not think of her but as slowly dying to the streaming away of her precious blood. What to do I knew not. And in addition to this dreadful state of despair was the obligation upon me to watch the boat, and shrewdly and seriously attend to my course by the warning suri-thunder floating back against the wind from the echoing strand. From time to time I would address Imogene, always with a terror in me of winning no reply, of touching her and finding her dead. Once she answered that she believed the bleeding in her shoulder had stopped; the icy coldness was gone, and there was a small smarting there as if she had been burnt, but nothing that she could not easily endure. But I knew by the tone of her voice that she spoke only to give me comfort; either that she was suffering above the power of her love for me to conceal in her faltering whispers, or that her strength was unequal to the labor of utterance.

Yet, as I have said, what could I do? I was no chirurgeon; and I wonder that my heart did not break to the bending of my scorching eyes upon my love lying wounded and bleeding at my feet.

An hour passed; the fog still compassed us, but the white splendor of the moon was upon it. Methought that I heard Imogene whisper. I dropped on my knee, and she asked for water. I let go the steering oar that jammed in the grummet and that could not therefore go adrift, and with great trouble found the little cup that I had hidden in one of the bags, and poured some water out of the pitcher into it. She moaned in pain when I put my arm under her head to raise it; but she drank greedily, nevertheless, and thanked me in a whisper when I tenderly let sink her head on to the jacket.

I resumed my place at the oar, and through the blackness drove the boat, the sail pulling briskly, the water shining very brightly in our wake, and, as my ear seemed to fancy, the noise of the surf dwindling somewhat, whence I conjectured we were hauling off the coast and standing more directly seaward. I do not know that I should have been without hope for my teloved if it had not been for the haunting and blasting thought that nothing but misery could attend association with Vanderdecken and his doomed ship. It seemed to me now—though on board I had been too eager to escape with her, too wrapped up in my love for such consideration to occupy my mind—that nothing less than the death of one of us could expiate our involuntary and unhappy connection with the banned and fated craft. Ships that spoke her perished, often with all hands; misfortunes pursued those who merely sighted her. What sort of death could the Curse involve for one who had lived for years or for weeks in the monstrous fabric, who had conversed familiarly with her abhorred occupants, who had been admitted into close inspection of her secret life, beheld the enactment by Vanderdecken in his sleep of the impious and horrible drama of his Christ-defying wrath, eat of his bread, drank of his cup, yea, and hearkened with sympathy to his talk of home, to his yearning speech concerning those he loved there?
Suddenly the fog broke up. It was then about 2 o'clock. The vapor floated into league-long streaks, lunar tinted here and there into an aerial mockery of the rainbow, and over the edge of one great steam-like body the moon, with an ice-like diamond splendor of radiance looked down upon us out of a pool of black sky. The lustre had something of the sharpness of daylight, only that the flooded pearl of it wore the complexion of death, all things showing out wan. And in that illumination the delicate gold of Imogene's hair melted into the extreme pallor of the forehead on which it stirred to the wind, and her lips were of the color of her cheeks, and her half-closed lids like wax.

I let go the ear to kneel and look at her. She lay so still, with such unheeding eyes that I made sure she was dead, and my brain reeled as though my heart had stopped.

I said hoarsely and hollowly, "Imogene."

The fringe of her eyelids trembled, and I marked a faint smile on her lips.

"Dearest," cried I, "how is it with thee?"

She returned no answer.

I said: "I shall be able to see the wound now, and perhaps check the bleeding. I can cut the dress clear of the shoulder and you need not stir."

She exclaimed—but, my God how feebly!—"Dearest, let me lie as I am," speaking with a sort of sigh between each word. And then she added, "Kiss me."

I pressed my lips to hers; they were cold as the mist that was passing away in wroaths and clouds. I saw how it was and let her have her way. It would have been cruel to touch her with more than my lips. And even though I should have cut away her apparel to the wound and saw it, what could I do? Suppose the bleeding internal—the bullet lodged within, the lung touched, or some artery severed?

LYNCHING IN STEELVILLE, MO. Lewis Davis, Who Murdered His Friend and Neighbor, Hanged by Masked Men.
Lewis Davis, who was under indictment for the murder of his friend and neighbor, David Mills, was taken from jail at Steelville, Mo., and lynched. The tragedy was of a sensational character. Davis, who had been in St. Louis for safe-keeping for six months, was returned to Steelville for trial. His case was to have been called the morning following his arrival. Three hours before daylight forty masked men rode into the town, and, after placing pickets on all the streets, leading to the jail, proceeded to attack the structure. Tools were secured from a blacksmith shop, and the doors were soon battered down. While the attack was in progress a Deputy Sheriff and one guard were captured. Davis fought like a demon. He knocked down four of the lynchers with a piece of bed-post. He was finally overpowered and with a rope around his neck was led out of town and lynched over the grave of Pat Wallace, who was lynched for the murder of the Logan family in 1886. Davis did not confess. The crime for which Davis was lynched was committed January 2. Davis and Miller started to town to pay their taxes. Miller's body was found with a bullet in the head and his pockets rifled. The bullet fitted Davis' pistol. It was a peculiar rifle bore, and the circumstantial evidence was strong against him.

Murder and Threatened Lynching.
Murder and Threatened Lynching.

WAUSEAU, Wis., Jan. 1.—Louis Butler was shot dead at 6 o'clock to-night by Louis Schlitz. The former owns the City Hotel and the latter the Hotel Northern. Butler had been going from saloon to saloon, with five companions, and engaged in a quarrel with Schlitz in the bar-room of the Hotel Northern because the latter refused to sell the party drinks. They grappled, and Schlitz drew a pistol and shot him. Schlitz hurried to the jail and surrendered himself. Several hundred men surrounded the jail, determined to lynch him. Sheriff Healey declared that he had a posses of men armed with Winchesters, and any hostile attempt would be met with a volley. The crowd then dispersed.

WARSAW, WIS., Jan. 2.—Larry Butler was shot through the heart last night by Louis Schlicht. The former owned the City hotel and the latter the Hotel Northern. Butler had been going from saloon to saloon and engaged in a quarrel with Schlicht in the barroom of the Hotel Northern because the latter refused to sell him drinks. They grappled and Schlicht drew his pistol and shot him. Schlicht hurried to the jail and surrendered himself. Several hundred men surrounded the jail determined to lynch him. Sheriff Healty declared that he had a posse of men armed and any hostile attempt would be met with a volley. The crowd then dispersed.

IS HELD FOR TRIAL
Landlord Schlicht Must Answer for killing Butter.
WAUSAU, Jan. 3.—Coroner Quandt this afternoon investigated the killing of Louis Butter. The inquest was held in the court house, which was crowded with people. The croner's jury consisted of M. M. Partrige, Herman Feldman, E. D. Pardee, S. T. Winkley, A. D. Collens and Henry Seim, Phillip Starder, Louis Ruder, Leo and Max Dahlman, Louis Secor, Charley, Williams and Wm. Kennedy, the parties who accompained Butter to the Northern hotel saloon, where the shooting occurred, all testified to substantially the same story, viz. That the party drove to the house in a sleigh and ordered drinks to be carried out to them; that Schlicht looked at the party and remarked "that was enough," and shut the door in their faces; that they then returned the team to the barn and, at the urgent solicitation of Williams, who boarded there, went back to the Northern hotel, entered the barroom, where Willaims called for the drinks, remarking to Schlicht that he was "a dandy;" that Schlicht retorted and that Butter then made vulgar and insulting reference to Schlicht; that Schlicht retorted with an epithet and advanced on Butter; that he struck Butter and then clinched with him, that Butter got Schlicht's head under his arm, and that the explosion of a pistol followed immediately, and Butter fell a corpse.

John Miller, Judge Marchetti and the Hon. John Ringle, who were in an adjoining room, testified that they saw the parties enter, and witnessed the affray. Judge Marchetti said Schlicht was in the room with him, and his companions, at the time the Butter party entered the bar-room, and did not believe he went behind the bar; that Schlicht threw up his hands when he encountered Butter, as though to warn him off and retreated from the bar to an adjoining room before shooting. Miller testified that Buttor said, while he had Schlicht's head in chancery, "You — —, I'll fix you." Sheriff Healy testified that Schlicht surrendered himself and gave the weapon to him at his office, and told him he had shot Butter. Dr. Wm. Wylie testified as to the character of the wound. The jury rendered a verdict in accordance with facts and recommended that Schlicht be held for trial.

Mr. Butter will be buried at 2 P. M. tomorrow under the auspices of the members of the Turnverein. Schlicht is still in jail and realizes the full enormity of his act. He says he is a ruined man. He is very restless, and will have his examination before Judge Crosby, who has just been appointed municipal judge by the governor, on Thursday. Public opinion as regards the shooting is divided.—[Sentinel.

louis-schlicht-wausau-1888-01-01.A13:
Charged With Murder.
Special to the Globe.
WAUSAU, Wis., Jan. 13.—Louis Schlecht was bound over to the circuit court this afternoon to answer to the charge of murder in the first degree. Schlecht shot and instantly killed Louis Butler on New Year's day. Schlecht claims the shooting was accidental, but the evidence is against the plea.
louis-schlicht-wausau-1888-01-01.A14:
His Bond Fixed.
Special to the Globe.
WAUSAU, Wis., Jan. 16.—The bond of Louis Schlecht, who shot and killed Louis Butler, was fixed to-day in the circuit court at $4,000. He will have no trouble in getting sureties and will be released from jail to-morrow.
louis-schlicht-wausau-1888-01-01.A16:
A Continuance Granted.
Special to the Globe.
WAUSAU, Wis., March 27.—Louis Schlecht was arraigned before the circuit court to-day charged with the murder of Louis Butler last New Year's day. He entered a plea of not guilty. He asked for a continuance until next term, which was granted.

Soldiers Prevent a Lynching.
BIRMINGHAM, Ala., Aug. 20.—A special from Alexandria City says the Alexandria City rifles were called out to prevent the lynching of Nathan M. Reed, a farmer, 60 years old, who is accused of wife murder. Reed is a prominent member of the Baptist church and an officer in several societies. He had been married thirty years and has several children grown. Recently he has been paying attention to his wife's young sister. Reed's wife accused him of intimacy with her sister, and he became so enraged that he caught her by the throat and choked her, from the effects of which she died. Reed was arrested, and the news of his crime caused intense excitement. A lynching party was organized, and only the presence of the military saved his life.
nathan-n-reed-alexandria-city-1888-08.A3:
Theratened With Lynching.
BIRMINGHAM, Ala., August 19.—[Special.]—A special from Alexandria City, seventy-two miles southeast of this city, says: Last evening the Alexandria City Rifles were called out to guard the jail to prevent the lynching of Nathan M. Reed, a farmer sixty years old, who is accused of wife murder. Reed is a prominent farmer and lived three miles from town. He is a prominent member of the Baptist church and an officer in several secret societies. He has been married thirty-five years and has several children grown. Recently he has been paying attention to his wife's sister, a young lady about twenty-five years old.

Yesterday morning Reed's wife accused him of intimacy with her sister, and he became so enraged that he caught her by the throat and choked her to the floor. Mrs. Reed was in delicate health, and last night died from the effects of her husband's cruel treatment. Reed was arrested and put in jail, and the news of his crime spread rapidly, causing intense excitement. A lynching party was quickly organized, and only the presence of the military at the jail saved Reed's life.

noah-griffin-ocheeshee-1888-08-18.A1:
A Negro Lynched.
[By telegraph to the Dispatch.]

APALACHICOLA, FLA., August 18.—A lynching took place at Ocheeshee, Calhoun county, Wednesday. Nash Griffin, a negro, wrote an insulting note to a young white lady, Miss Kimmie Griffin. She showed the note to some male friends, who caught Griffin, gave him one hundred lashes, and ordered him to leave the county. He did not go, when forty masked men caught him and shot him to death. No arrests have been made.

THE SOUTHERN END OF IT.
Two Negroes Lynched and a White Man Shot Fatally.
SHREVEPORT, La., Aug. 20.—A negro was lynched near Big Cypress bayou in Bossier parish, on Tuesday, for stealing some money from a store at that place.

APALACHICOLA, Fla., Aug. 20.—A lynching took place at Ocheehee, Calhoun county on Wednesday. Noah Griffin, a negro wrote an insulting note to a young white lady, Miss Simmie Griffin. She showed the note to some white men, who caught Griffin, gave him 190 lashes and ordered him to leave the county. He did not go, when a gang of forty men caught and shot him to death. No arrests have been made.

NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 20.—Dr. W. F. Simmons, an ex-member of the legislature, was shot twice in his store, twelve miles east of Osyke, Miss., Saturday by Lee Hinson. His wounds are pronounced fatal. Hinson and two others who were present at the shooting were lodged in jail. Simmons had taken a very decided stand against the practice of "regulating," and thus incurred the enmity of Hinson and others.

In the Senate on the 15th a resolution was passed calling on the Secretary of the Treasury for a statement of the amounts deposited in National banks on August 1, 1888. The fisheries treaty was further discussed...In the House the time was occupied in considering the Fortification bill.

In the Senate on the 16th the conference report on the Army Appropriation bill was agreed to and the fisheries treaty was further discussed...In the House the Fortification Appropriation bill was passed, but all efforts to transact any other business were defeated because of the lack of a quorum.

A BILL was passed in the Senate on the 17th prohibiting the mailing of obscene or libelous matter in transparent envelopes. It was agreed to vote on the fisheries treaty next Tuesday. Adjourned to the 20th...In the House filibustering tactics on a proposition to assign certain days for the consideration of general pension legislation and to take up the General Deficiency bill consumed most of the session.

DOMESTIC.

HEALTH officers at Buffalo, N. Y., on the 15th stopped a public funeral, it having come to their knowledge that the death resulted from small-pox.

The great brick-makers' strike in Chicago collapsed on the 15th, owing to union men at work refusing longer to support the strikers.

SAMPLES of gold from the Vermillion mine at Sunbury, Mich., assayed $25,000 to $75,000 a ton at Sault Ste Marie on the 15th.

WEAVERS in the linen-mill at Fall River, Mass., went on a strike on the 15th, and two thousand looms were idle.

SAMUEL NISHAM, aged thirteen years, of Camden, Pa., who was bitten by a dog July 4, died on the 16th inst. of hydrophobia.

JAMES JONES and Joseph Rosenberg, Louisville policemen, attempted on the 16th to arrest Charles Dilger, a desperado who was beating his mistress, when Dilger fought them with a knife, stabbing both fatally.

The National convention of Insurance Commissioners in session on the 16th at Madison, Wis., elected O. F. Tyler, of Connecticut, president.

NINE persons were injured in a collision on the 16th on the Illinois Central railroad at South Lawn, a Chicago suburb.

CHIEF MESCOTT, of the Kickapoos, his squaw and five children were killed by lightning on the 16th in his cabin on the reservation near Netawaka, Kan.

ADOLPH HARMAN, a German clerk at Navasink, N. J., tried to shoot Mrs. Hayes, his mother in-law, on the 16th, and then killed his wife and himself. Jealousy was the cause.

LEADING heavy hardware jobbers of the West met in Chicago on the 16th and organized a National union of heavy hardware jobbers, the object being to oppose the formation of trusts, combinations and syndicates as connected with the business. J. J. Parkhurst, of Chicago, was elected president.

The Supreme Court of Wyoming Territory on the 16th decided that woman suffrage in the Territory was unconstitutional.

FREDERICK VON OBERKAMPF, the Chicago mail-box robber, said on the 16th that there was an international band of mail thieves in existence, and one Charles Edwards was implicated at the head and front of the gang.

Advices of the 16th from Jacksonville showed that the yellow-fever epidemic had been checked in that city, but the panic which resulted throughout the South had not subsided.

The steamers Geiser and Thingvalla of the Thingvalla trans-Atlantic line collided in a fog off Sable Island on the 14th inst., and one hundred and nineteen persons were drowned. The Geiser sank in five minutes after the accident. Some of the passengers and crew escaped to the Thingvalla, which was also badly injured and threatened to go down, when the steamer Wieland came to the rescue. The Wieland arrived at the port of New York with the survivors on the 16th. The Thingvalla put into Hallifax.

The North Chicago rolling-mills, at South Chicago, shut down on the 16th for an indefinite period, throwing out of employment some fifteen hundred men.

CONSIDERABLE damage was reported on the 15th to rice and sugar crops in Louisiana by a heavy wind and rain-storm, which was most severe at Bayou Sara, Baton Rouge and along the Mississippi gulf coast.

A heavy frost fell in Northern Minnesota and Dakota on the 17th.

During the seven days ended on the 17th there were 151 business failures in the United States, against 186 the previous seven days. The total failures in the United States from January 1 to date is 6,428, against 6,132 in 1887.

The National Commandery of the Sons of Veterans in session on the 17th at Wheeling, W. Va., elected as Commander-in-Chief George R. Abbott, of Illinois.

During the absence of Henry Shropshire and his wife from their home near Columbia, S. C., on the 17th the house was burned and their two little children perished in the flames.

Hugh Blachman was hanged at Little Rock, Ark., on the 17th for the murder of a friend in May last, and Alexander Wood (colored) was executed at Blackfoot, I. T., for the murder of his wife in March, 1887.

While digging a well on the 17th near Steubenville, O., George Owens and his son were killed, and Mrs. Owens died soon after from the shock.

Admiral Luce received orders on the 17th to proceed to Port au Prince, Hayti, to protect American interests in the Haytien waters, on account of the state of martial law which exists.

At the meeting of the American Bar Association on the 17th at Saratoga, N. Y., David Dudley Field, of New York, was elected president, and General Harrison, of Indianapolis, one of the vice presidents.

The National Association of Fire Engineers in session at Minneapolis on the 17th elected F. L. Stetson, of that city, president.

The Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers met at Detroit on the 17th to celebrate the twenty-fifth anniversary of their organization. Over two thousand members were present.

At North Adams, Mass., on the 17th Mrs. Joseph McDay and Miss Kate Armstrong were burned to death as a result of starting
AT North Adams, Mass., on the 17th Mrs. Joseph McDay and Miss Kate Armstrong were burned to death as a result of starting a fire with kerosene.

The race war in Vermillion, New Iberia and Lafayette parishes in Louisiana culminated on the 17th in the killing of thirteen negroes.

The store of Wallace & Kelly, at West Charleston, W. Va., was burned on the 17th, and Simon Wallace and his mother, who were sleeping over the store, perished in the flames.

DEACON LOVERING, aged ninety years, and his sister and housekeeper, Mrs. Richardson, were instantly killed by lightning on the 17th at Greenfield, Mass., and the farm-house, barns and buildings were burned.

DISPATCHES of the 17th say that the total number of persons lost in the recent collision between the steamers Thingvalla and Geiser was one hundred and eighteen. The loss of the Geiser and cargo was placed at $450.000.

GREAT excitement was created on the 17th at the Newport iron and steel mills, just across the river from Cincinnati, by the discovery of seventeen dynamite bombs in a pile of scrap-iron.

THREE robbers held up a Union Pacific passenger train on the 18th near Cheyenne, Wy. T., but the train men showed fight and drove them off.

noah-griffin-ocheeshee-1888-08-18.A16: Last week Noah Griffin wrote an insulting letter to a white woman in Ocheehees, Fla. She showed the note to some white men, who caught Griffin and gave him one hundred lashes and ordered him to leave the county. He did not go, and a mob of forty masked men took him and shot him to death. No arrests have been made. That Griffin did wrong to write the note we admit; but we will venture the assertion that there was not one man among that forty who murdered him, who coined any of them could, but has been guilty of the same offense. And it certainly was not a crime worthy of death. And we would willingly stake our hope of heaven, that there was not one of them, who had not insulted some Colored woman, in a much more flagrant manner, without even so much as thinking he had done anything wrong. A pure white woman is not one whit better than a pure Colored one, and it is no more wrong for a Colored man to make improper advances to a white woman than it is for a white man to make improper advances to a Colored one. Yet, there are ninety-nine instances where white men insult Colored women to one where Colored men insult white ones. The superior (?) race ought to set a better example in regard to morals and justice. The trouble in the above mentioned case was not because a man had insulted a woman, but because the accused was Colored and the accuser white. Whenever the criminal is black and the victim white the criminal is worse than the crime.

At Guide Rock, Neb., Billy Cole, who shot William Montgomery and Charles Grant at a dance Aug. 17, was taken from jail by twelve masked men at 2 o'clock Monday morning, and hanged on the railroad bridge.

At Superior, Wis., Sunday, ex-Chief of Police Richard Collins shot and seriously wounded his wife, who was at the residence of James Myers, and wounded Myers, who, in return, shot Collins in the head. Jealousy was the cause.

Mrs. Christina Keefer and her married daughter, Lena Witheim, were arrested at Terre Haute, Ind., Monday for raising dollar-notes to ten by clipping the cipher from cigar-box stamps and pasting it next the figure 1. They had succeeded in passing several of them.

An easterly gale has prevailed in New Orleans and vicinity since Saturday night. Several buildings were unroofed, fences blown down, trees uprooted, and the Pittsburg and Southern coal combination lost fifty vessels valued at $3,000 each. Nashville and Illinois Central trains were delayed by washouts. Great damage has been done to rice and sugar cane crops.

Mrs. Norton, who eloped with Editor Moore from St. Louis, is reported to have settled with her husband and released all claim on his property.

Noah Griffin, a negro, was shot dead by forty masked men at Ocheches, Fla., last Wednesday for writing insulting notes to a white girl.

Dr. A. K. Fisher, a German writer and politician of Indianapolis and the son-in-law of Dr. Brock of Chicago, killed himself with opium Saturday night.

William and Louis Nagler, ranchers of Pleasant Valley, Arizona, have been lynched, and W. McRaigy, employed on the Aztec Land and Cattle company's ranch there has been driven out of Holbrook, Arizona, by outlaws.

Dr. W. F. Simmons, an ex-member of the legislature, was fatally shot at Osyka, Miss., Saturday by Lee Henson, who with two confederates are in jail. Simmons had incurred their enmity by opposing "regulating."

Warden McClaughrey, of Joliet prison, has been offered the wardenship of the new Pennsylvania reformatory at Huntington, Pa., with a salary of $1,000, a furnished house, servants, etc. It is thought he will accept the place.

Masked men attempted to rob a Union Pacific express near Dana Station, Wyoming early Friday morning, but were beaten off by the train hands. Many shots were fired and a brakeman was wounded.

Martin L. Lewis, alias Thomas Saunders, alias Thomas Lovejoy, was arrested at Battle Creek, Mich., for an attempt to pass a forged check of the First national bank of southern Kansas. Checks aggregating $1,000 on the same bank were found on his person. He pleaded guilty.

The investigation of the White Caps by Attorney-General Michener of Indiana has resulted in one of the gang turning State's evidence. He charges the order with being influenced in their act by revenge for private wrongs. The headquarters of the order is near English. The White Caps have issued a circular threatening to resist the State's investigation with bloodshed.

Mrs. H. E. Brown, charged with poisoning at Mason City, Iowa, was acquitted at the close of the preliminary examination Saturday.

Hamilton S. Weeks, representing a Western company, has secured the right to establish graphophone exchanges in the territory east of the Rocky Mountains and west of the Mississippi, and the instruments will be introduced in the leading cities of that District by Oct. 1.

Another rate war has broken out, which bids fair to affect the passenger business of every road from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The Central Friday announced a cut in first and second class fares from Chicago to St. Paul from $11.50 and $9.00 to $6.40 and $5 respectively.

At Kalamazoo, Mich., Thursday evening, James O'Brien, becoming infuriated at his sweetheart Jennie Smith, beat and chooked her so severely that she will probably die.

At Woodland, Wis., Thursday George Moon, aged 23, shot and killed Jennie Woolver, a domestic employed on William Sletyer's farm, then kissed her and killed himself. He had lately returned from Colorado and found the girl another's promised wife.

old-man-kelly-harold-1888-01-02.A2:
CONFESSED HIS CELLS.
Old Man Kelly. Overtaken by Vigilantes and Lynched. WINSTON, KAN. January 3. — Further
WICHITA, KAN., January 3 — Further details of the lynching of the notorious Kelly family have reached here. After the killing of the mother and son, the vigilantes started in pursuit of the old man, who had escaped on horsback.

After three hours' hard driving they overtook him. Kelly was told that he had but a few minutes to live, and was given permission to make any statement he desired. He said:

"I moved to Kansas from the mountains of Pennsylvania in 1879, and lived at different points along the southern border until I decided to move to No Man's Land. I settled 25 miles from Beaver City, and went into the cattle business. Soon after I opened a sort of a tavern. Several persons disappeared while passing along this trail, but as to their death I have nothing to say. A good deal of talk of foul play was made, and I determined to move on to South Texas."

The old man was then strung up for a few minutes and let down again, when he confessed that he and his family had killed and robbed nine men and two women. He was then strung up again and left hanging.
old-man-kelly-harold-1888-01-02.A4:
A TERROR HANGED.
Kelly the Murderer Caught t and Confesses His Crime
LITTLE ROCK, Jan. 3.—A special to
Kelly the Murderer Caught and Confesses His Crime

LITTLE ROCK, Jan. 3.—A special to the Gazette from Harold, Texas, last evening, give the particulars of the capture and punishment of the elder Kelly, the only survivor of the notorious Kelly family of No-Man's-land. The history of their crime and of the capture and death at the hands of vigilantes of Mrs. Kelly and of the son and daughter have already been published. The old man, however, made his escape when the other members of the family paid the penalty for their crime, but the vigilantes, it seems, followed and caught him and he was immediately informed that he had but a short time to live and that anything he had to say would be heard. He threw a furtive glance at the speaker and asked about the rest, meaning his wife and children. The leader without a word cast a look upward, pointing to the limb of a tree.

The old man understood and commenced talking in an almost inaudible voice and made a brief statement about as follows: "I moved to Kansas from the mountains in Pennsylvania in 1869 and lived at different points along the southern border of that state until I decided to move to No-Man's-Land. I located some twenty five miles from Beaver City and went into the cattle business. Soon after locating I opened up a sort of tavern and entertained travelers. Several persons disappeared while passing along this trail, but as to their death I have nothing to say. A good deal of talk and suspicion of foul play was heard and I determined to move on south to Texas. This is all I have to say. If they were killed at my house it was done without me knowing it."

A few words were spoken by members of the band aside, when preparations were at once made to hang him. A rope was placed around his neck, and in a short time the body of Kelly, with his hands tied behind his back, was swinging in the air.
He was then let down and asked to confess his crimes. This he did in a brief way. He said all the members of his family were equally guilty. He said in all they had killed and robbed nine men and two women. He told where the money was hidden that had been taken, and gave up what he had on his person. He professed not to know where the murdered parties came from. He was again swung up and left to hang.
On his person was found a gold watch bearing the initials, "I. A. T." Taylor was the name of one of the missing men.

CAPTURED THE GANG.
The Kelly Family, Rivals of the Benders, Receive Their Due Reward.
Confession By the Old Man--The Horrible Discovery.
A CHARNAL HOUSE.
wholesale murder of travelers by the Kelly family in their "dug out" tavern, in "No Man's Land," on the line between Meade Center, Kansas, and Beaver City, as already chronicled, have taken on fresh interest since the reports received here of the manner of the taking off of the Kelly's. Kelly's house was arranged very much after the fashion of that used by the notorious Benders, except that at the Kelly place the visitor was seated in a chair over a trap door, which door would be opened suddenly, precipitating the victim into a cellar, where he could be dispatched at leisure.

About the middle of December Kelly's house was shut up, and no one could tell what had become of the inmates. Soon came inquiry from a Chicago firm for a missing drummer, and he was traced to the Kelly retreat, but no further. A close scrutiny of the premises led to the breaking down of the door of the house, when the dead body of the missing man was found in the cellar, nearly eaten up by rats. There were also five other bodies found in this pit of hell, but all in varying states of decomposition, from decaying, rat-eaten flesh, to the ghastly, grinning skeleton. Besides these, there were four bodies found buried beneath the stable, one of which was that of a woman about thirty years of age. Lying alongside of the barn, buried at a depth of not over three feet, was unearthed the remains of a man which appeared to be better dressed than any of the others. At the corner of the barn were buried the bodies of a third man and woman, whose heads were crushed as though from a blow with some heavy instrument. In the woodshed was found a blunt ax, upon which were still plainly visible particles of flesh and human hair, as well as clots of blood. No one knew where the family were, but one thing was certain—they were gone.

MAKING THEIR ESCAPE.

When information of the ghastly find was brought to Beaver City, it was recollected that the Kelly family, consisting of the old man, William, aged about fifty-five years; "Billy," a son of twenty; "Kit," the old man's wife, and "Kit," the twenty-year-old daughter, had only a few days before passed through town en route, as they said, to New Mexico. They were driving a span of horses and leading four others, and seemed to have plenty of money. A posse of twenty citizens was at once made up and started in pursuit.

The trail led along the north bank of Palo Duro creek. As the race continued it was found that the villains had changed their course south, toward Wheeler county, Texas, for which point they were evidently aiming. From returning wagons on the road it was also ascertained that the parties wanted were not far in the lead. About noon on Thursday last they were seen, and at once seemed to discover their pursuers, as they left the wagon and at once mounted the horses which they had been leading. From this time until two hours later a hot chase was had, when the horse ridden by Mrs. Kelly stumbled and fell, breaking its own neck. No stop was made by either party on account of the incident, and about a half hour later the pursuing band of vigilantes were near enough to the son and daughter to shoot. A cry of "halt" brought them to a stop, but the old man, who rode a better animal, kept on his way.

THE HANGING.

Upon the pursuers coming up with "Bill" and "Kit," and surrounding them, the girl began at once begging for mercy and saying she "never killed anybody." It was of no use. The evidence was too conclusive, and besides Bill said:

"Oh, shut up! It isn't any use, Kit. You've got to go with me. You know you had just as much to do about it as I."

Ropes were speedily procured and the two bound. There was no ceremony. One of the party climbed a tree and slipped two ropes over one of the outstretched branches. At the ends two running nooses had been made. The murderers were then placed beneath them and the ropes adjusted about their necks in true hangman style. They were given a chance to pray or make any statement they desired. There was no such thing as repentance in either of the condemned.

“Let her go,” said the boy; “I’ve had my share of fun.”

“Shall I tell?” half whispered the girl to her brother.

“No, —— —— them; let them find out for themselves,” was the reply.

The girl nodded assent, and in a moment the two bodies were hanging suspended in the air.

The ropes were tied to an adjoining sapling and the bodies left hanging, while the posse rode on after the old man Kelly, who, by this time, had disappeared from sight.

ATTEMPTED MURDER.
OLNEY, Ill., Feb. 14.—This afternoon Sheriff Lee Gowens, of Lawrence county, and a posse composed of Constable Propes John Milburn and Ben Fisher, took the Ohio and Mississippi passenger train at Lawrenceville to come to Olney in search of the two tramps who attempted the murder of old Mr. and Mrs. David Potter, for their money at their home near Lawrence last night. When the train was two miles west of Claremont a station on the road east of here, Milburn, looking out of the car window, noticed four men crossing a field. The conductor, Jas. Stanton, stopped the train and let the sheriff and party off. They went back and at the point of a revolver placed the four men under arrest and brought them to this city and lodged them in jail. The tramps had four revolvers and three knives. One of the latter showed signs of blood. They deny all knowledge of the affair. The prisoners hail from St. Louis, and will be taken to Lawrenceville tonight.
porter-family-lawrenceville-1888-02-16.A2:
STILL ANOTHER.
Burglars Seem to be Over-Running All Illinois State.
SPRINGFIELD, Ill., February 15.—D. S. Porter, a wealthy farmer, well known throughout this State, and his wife, had a terrible encounter with burglars, Sunday night, near Lawrenceville. Early in the evening, Mr. Porter responded to a knock at the door, when a man entered and placed a revolver at his head. He threw his assailant to the floor, and, while struggling with him, a second man entered and held Mrs. Porter at bay with a revolver. She went at this one with a poker while her husband struggled with the first. Two more of the gang came into the assistance of their confederates and a terrible fight ensued. Some of the neighbors became alarmed by this time, and the burglars made a hurried departure. Mr. and Mrs. Porter were badly and perhaps fatally injured. He had received numerous deep cuts from a knife and she was injured internally, besides being badly burned from seizing the wrong end of the poker. The Sheriff, with the whole town for a posse, is making a vigorous search for the gang.

Mr. Smith is a traveled young man of thirty, and the son of a large blanket manufacturer of Halifax. He has been in India and visited almost every part of the world. When Mr. Carter was in England this summer, Smith took him to his house and treated him as one of the family, hence the present visit is simply an exchange of courtesies.

James Shells, of New York, is a boss bricklayer and contractor, and the only man of color belonging to the union of mechanics of that profession there. He is a young man, about twenty-six years of age, and is making rapid strides in North Carolina, where he learned his trade. He had to board himself on $150 a year, or fifty cents per day. In New York he demanded five dollars per day, and recently he passed a Civil Service Board examination, and has been appointed inspector of the Great Aqueduct at a salary of $2,100. It is, without a doubt, one of the greatest pieces of engineering and masonry work ever attempted in the city. It is a large tunnel, 200 feet in circumference, 100 feet in diameter, and is fifty miles long, extending from Croton Lake to New York City.

pres-sans-moscow.A3:
Wasn't Even an Honest Negro.
St. Louis, Oct. 1.—Miss Hattie Flack, the St. Louis girl who married a notorious negro in Jacksonville, Ill., two weeks ago, was arrested yesterday in Moscow, Ky., and returned here in charge of an officer. The girl was 18 years of age, and was on a visit to her father, from whence the elopement occurred. The negro, Press Sams, proves to be a horse thief, and is now a fugitive in Kentucky.

SHE MARRIED THE NEGRO COACHMAN, AND HE HAS PROBABLY BEEN LYNCHED.

Says a special to the Philadelphia Press from St. Louis, Oct. 1: D.C. McCoy, a deputy sheriff, who left Jacksonville, Ill., last week on the trail of Press Sams, the negro who was married to a white woman, Miss Hattle Flack, about two weeks ago, near Jacksonville, arrived with the woman in his custody and turned her over to her father, Charles E. Flack, of Schreiver, Flack & Co. commission merchants, of this city. McCoy, who is an old friend of the family, found the couple at a log cabin in the mountains, near Clinton, living with the family of Sams' brother-in-law. The girl at first refused to go with McCoy, until he convinced her that Sams had another wife from whom he had never been divorced. McCoy refuses to say what became of Sams, but intimates that he was lynched to save the state the expense of his trial for bigamy. The report given out at Clinton is that Sams has left the country. The Flack family live near Jacksonville, and Sams was their coachman.
pres-sans-moscow.A6:
Miss Flack's Infatuation.
CLINTON, Ky., Oct. 2.—Miss Flack, the daughter of a St. Louis merchant, who married Press Sams, a negro, at Jacksonville, Ills., a short time ago, who has since deserted her, was arrested at Moscow, Saturday night, in the house of Jim Gholson, a negro brother-in-law of Press Sams. She refused to go with the officers until she learned that a warrant for her was in their possession. She was taken to St. Louis.
pres-sans-moscow.A8:
She Repents Her Folly.
St. Louis, Mo., Oct. 1.—Hattie Flack, the nineteen year old daughter of Charles E. Flack, of the St. Louis commission house of Shirmir & Flack, who married a mulatto named Pres Sams, the hired man on her father's farm near Jacksonville, Ill., is at home again. She was brought to St. Louis and turned over to her parents by Deputy Sheriff McCoy, of Jacksonville, who found her near Moscow, Ky. Sams fled to escape lynching. It transpires that the negro was a married man when he induced Miss Flack to wed him. The girl now bitterly repents her folly.

A visitor from Louisville, Ky., was found dead in a small building near the city of Hot Springs, Monday evening. His name was Granville Cazee.

Mattie Flack, a wealthy merchant's daughter of St. Louis, ran away last week and married a mulatto named Sams who was hired on her father's farm near Jacksonville, Ill. She was overtaken by the deputy sheriff and brought back home. Sams has another wife, and made his escape, or he would have been lynched.

The project of admitting Utah into the Union as one of the States is still further postponed. The commissioners reccomended it to be postponed until the Mormons show by their acts that they are willing to give up their ideas of polygamy entirely and live in accordance with civilized customs and laws. This is as it should be. The Mormons will come around all right after awhile.

The Wheelers' Aid Association of Columbia county had their regular meeting in the court house at this place on last Saturday, Sept. 29th, 1888. The by-laws, as submitted by the chairman on that committee with various alterations and some additions were adopted.

The initiation fee was reduced to 25 cents.

The Association elected officers for the ensuing year, which result was as follows: J. B. Roper, president; J. A. Sewell, vice president; J. D. Zachry, treasurer; T. J. Wesson, secretary.

The association will have its regular quarterly meetings, for the present at this place, the next to be the 4th Saturday in Dec., but there will be a call meeting at this place the 4th Saturday in this month, it being the 27th.

All Wheelers of Columbia county that are in good standing to join the association, and make it like the "Wheel of value to the farmer."

We will publish the proceedings of the last meeting in next issue.

press-neal-el-dorado-1888-09-08.A1:
A VOTE OR A LIFE IN ARKANSAS.
SIXTEEN MEN KILLED IN UNION COUNTY.
PREMEDITATED MURDER OF NEGROES AT THE POLLS-DEATH AND DISFRANCHISEMENT AT THE MUZZLE OF A GUN.
AT THE MUZZLE OF A GUN.

St. Louis, Sept. 12 (Special).—A dispatch from Little Rock says: "A reign of terror has succeeded the election outrages in Union County. Eldorado is the county seat. There is neither railroad nor telegraph in Union, Camden and Magnolia. The nearest railroad points are in adjoining counties. The statement of what has occurred in Union County was obtained from responsible white citizens of the county who have just come from there. The week before the election the Democrats visited and wrecked the printing office from which the union labor newspaper had been issued up to that time. On the Saturday night before the election they called upon the leading colored men who were going to vote for Norwood, and warned each one that if he persisted in voting on Monday he would be whipped or killed. To show that they were in earnest the Democrats took out twenty-five negroes representing nearly all of the precincts in the county and flogged them. On Sunday they went to a colored church, killed one negro and wounded several. At 6 o'clock Monday morning 100 white men armed with guns and pistols assembled at Eldorado to direct the election. By the time the polls opened they had killed one negro and whipped another so severely that he will probably die. Whenever a negro came in sight they would ride up to him and punch him with a gun, and warn him off with insulting epithets. This kind of work was kept up all day. When it was over the white men who had been witnesses to the outrages and were known to oppose such things were visited and at the muzzle of a gun were made to promise that they would not prosecute any of the perpetrators.

"Another Union County white man who is here trying to make arrangements to leave there permanently says: 'Every road to Eldorado was guarded with armed men on election day. As the negroes came in they were met and driven back. Unless they struck a trot homeward they were shot or whipped. Jordan Gray was made to pull off his shirt and was then pounded with guns and prodded with the bayonets. He is in bed now. It was reported when I left the county that sixteen persons had been killed since Sunday evening. You never saw so many scared people. A negro was killed at Lisbon on election day. At Champaignolle the ballot box was stolen by the Democrats at noon."
