press-neal-el-dorado-1888-09-08.A2:
The Race War in Arkansas.
LITTLE ROCK, Ark . Sept. 13.—It is reported from Union county that on Saturday night before the election twenty-five negroes, representing nearly all the precincts in the county, were taken out and flogged. On election day the negroes were warned away from the polls at the muzzles of shotguns, and several were beaten and killed. One white man reports that sixteen negroes were killed about election time.
press-neal-el-dorado-1888-09-08.A4:
BLOODY FRAUD IN ARKANSAS Charges of Murder, Outrage and Wholesale Fraud in the Late Election. Labor Men Shot Down—Democratic Clubs Said to Have Been Armed with State Rifles Gov. Hughes Accused of Complicity.
That the election in Arkansas on the 3d inst. was attended with more or less disturbance was briefly noted in the telegraphic returns on the following day. The Union Labor party failed to carry the State, and but little was said about the means used by the Democrats to defeat it. A letter from Mr. R. B. Carl Lee, a prominent leader of the Union Labor party and its principal candidate for Congress two years ago, contains a story of murder, outrage and fraud so startling that it is almost incredible. The letter was received in this city yesterday, and it is as follows:

"St. Louis, Mo., Sept. 14.

"G. W. Pike, New York City:

"Dear Sir and Brother—I am just from Arkansas. If the people of the United States only knew half how we have been treated Congress would wipe out the fraudulent State government in Arkansas and grant us a republican form of government as guaranteed by the federal Constitution.

"In Arkansas county they robbed us of the ballot-boxes at two townships with over 500 majority for us. In Union county Governor Hughes armed the Democratic clubs with the State Winchesters on the night before the election (Sunday). They paraded over the county and whipped over twenty colored men, some of them so badly that they had to keep their beds. On Monday they shot and killed seven white Union Labor men and wounded over twenty more, and at Eldorado, the county-seat, they took the poll books away from the judges and burned them before the eyes of the people and then held a new election at which no Union Labor man was permitted to vote.

"In Miller county the Democratic clubs were armed by Governor Hughes with the State's arms, and they went to the strong Union Labor precincts and notified them that if they voted the Union Labor ticket they would kill them. In Woodruff county they added over 1,000 votes to the Democratic vote, and defrauded us out of the election. In Crittenden county we had over 2,000 majority, this they cut down to less than 250. A delegation of white Wheelers immediately went to Little Rock and waited on Governor Hughes, giving him the facts, but he refused to take any action in the matter.

"In Lee county we had over 2,300 majority; this they counted for our opponents. In Mississippi county they changed 500 votes in the same way. In St. Francis county, at Blackfish, they stacked their guns around the voting place and refused to let the Union Labor people vote. At another township there they stuffed the ballot-box, and refused to let our men vote, when one of our men fired on them with squirrel shot, slightly wounding four of them. This is the only act of violence we are accused of in the State. I am sorry for this one.

"In Jackson county they secretly swindled us out of over 1,000 votes. In Lincoln county they changed over 500 of our votes to them. In Howard county the same. In Lafayette county they stole over 400 votes from us by throwing them out. In Little River county they stole from 500 to 800 votes from us by counting us out. In Garland county about the same number in the same way. In Saline county they stole over 400 votes from us by changing. In Lonoke county, Eaglis's home, they refused to count Williams township, that gave us 352 majority. In Pope county they changed 400 or 500 votes, perhaps more, from our candidate to their candidate. In Conway county they stole 700 or 800 in the same way.

"In Monroe county, at Pine Ridge, they forced the negroes to vote the Democratic ticket, saying: 'This is the ticket you have got to vote today.' In Pulaski county, the county in which Little Rock is situated, they stole nine ballot-boxes and refused to count two others—a loss to us of over 3,000 votes. Besides this, they changed the votes in many of the other wards, so that they gave them, instead of us, a majority.

"We undoubtedly carried the State and have been counted out. Our candidates are contesting, but I fear we can do nothing but show to the world the fraud that has been committed in a legal way, because the same fraud that gave them the State also gave them the Legislature; and it has to be tried before that body. You can use this letter as you see fit. Mind that it is not the Republicans that have been counted out, but the Union Labor ticket. The Republicans counted the Democrats out while they were in power, and now the Democrats count everybody out that is opposed to them. They have armed the Democratic clubs and made militia companies of them. No matter what our strength may be, we can never get it counted until the general government forces them to give us an honest election.

"Until then the shotgun and Winchester rifle in the hands of Democratic clubs and backed by the State officials (and they are backed by the United States government), rule in Arkansas, and not the people. Yours fraternally,

"R. B. CARL LEE."
press-neal-el-dorado-1888-09-08.A5:
How Arkansas Was Carried.
Fuller information just received.
How Arkansas Was Carried.

Fuller received, says the New York Mail and Express, confirms all that had been suspected about the way Arkansas was carried for Gov. Eagle by the Democrats. Crittenden county went Democratic for the first time since the war, showing a "change" of 3,000 votes—a change produced by banishing all the prominent negroes, including the county judge, the county clerk and other important officials; by whipping two dozen negroes and serving notice on the rest that they would attempt to vote on peril of their lives, and by intimidation and violence at the polls. Pulaski county was "carried," after a Republican majority of 2,000 had been polled, by breaking into the county clerk's office at Little Rock and stealing the returns from nine Republican precincts. This theft has been badly denounced by Gov. Hughes and other Democratic officials, but no efforts have been made to find out the perpetrators.

Union county, on the southern border of the state, a region in which there is not a single railway, was carried by the most open violence. The Union Labor newspaper office at the county seat, El Dorado, was wrecked the week before election. Negroes were stripped and whipped. A colored church was entered and one negro was killed, another mortally wounded, and still others severely injured. A correspondent of the Globe Democrat, who has been of his information from responsible white citizens of Union county, thus describes the scene at one of the polling places: "In Champagnole precinct, state militia, which had been organized after the militia, which had been organized after the polls and formed two lines. Every voter had to march up to the polls between the ranks of armed men. This was one of the precincts which would have given Norwood a large majority. About noon the Norwood ticket had, according to the tally, 102 ahead of the Democratic ticket. At this time three men with their heads covered with bandana masks marched up to the polls between the two lines of armed men, seized the ballot-box, marched back between the militia ranks and proceeded to destroy the box and its contents, no one molesting them. When the bandana Ku klux first laid hold of the box at the polling place, one of the judges of election resisted. The Ku klux drew a pistol, put it to the judge's head and soon quitted him. When the masked men got beyond the militia line they fired their guns and proceeded to destroy the box. After this episode the Democrats opened another poll, at which only Democrats voted. The night Mr. Cook, a merchant, an old Conferrate and one of the leading citizens of Champagnole, also had
the Democrats opened another poll, at which only Democrats voted. That night Mr. Cook, a merchant, an old Confederate and one of the leading citizens of Champagne, who had been an avowed supporter of Norwood, had his store and all his goods burned. A majority of about 500 was given Eagle, where there would have been a majority of at least 200 for Norwood with a free ballot and a fair count.

Further testimony is furnished by the Democratic organ at the state capital, the Little Rock Gazette, which prints a despatch from Arkansas county, saying: "Last night we had the disgraceful scene of eight heavily armed men escorting the ballot box in Prairie Township. They swore they would have the stolen box of Old River counted or have blood, but when they saw the determined stand of the Democrats they failed to put their threat into execution. The official count today gives Eagle a majority of 332 over Norwood. The whole state and county Democratic ticket are elected by a small majority, this by leaving out Old River Township, which is strongly Wheeler. The Wheeler will contest. Brickell, Democrat, received a majority of 43 over Langston, Republican, in this county for state senator. Everything quiet.

This Old River box was taken in charge by one Mr. T. L. Krier, who started for the county seat with it. He was stopped on the way by three masked men who took the ballot box from him, and it has never been heard from since. There was about 310 majority for the Republican-Wheeler candidates in the box. Without the votes of this township, the returns show a Democratic majority in the county of from 116 to 150.

These are samples of the methods by which Arkansas was carried for the Democratic candidates. What do Northern Democrats think of these things? It is
press-neal-el-dorado-1888-09-08.A6:
THE USUAL DEMOCRATIC FATE.
Just now, in Mahaska county, is presented the lovely spectacle of the Democrats coddling the colored voter in the most loving way. "The negro is a very prolific animal," says Allen G. Thurman, the Democratic Vice Presidential nominee, and every epithet of ignomy that Democratic lips could coin for a century stands behind that insult to the colored race.

The Mahaska Democrts, or some of them, stand now as great lovers of the negro. At the same time these Democrats endorse the acts of the Arkansas Democrats at the recent election, and say that under the same circumstances they would do the same.

What are the "circumstances"? Well, simply this: The Republicans carried several of the counties in that State in past elections. To keep the colored voters from the polls the most devilish schemes of murder and cruelty were invented, and this is what happened, and we quote only the report on the election in Union county. This county is on the Louisiana line, and is one of the largest in the State. A reliable citizen and Republican, white, makes the following report—he having been a supporter of the Union Labor candidate, Norwood, for Governor:

Saturday, Sept. 1, Norwood and Eagle spoke at El Dorado. Everything was remarkably quiet, but Saturday night the marauding and whipping of colored men began. Wherever the Democrats thought whipping some influential colored man would scare the rest of the neighborhood
but Saturday night the marauding and whipping of colored men began. Wherever the Democrats thought whipping some influential colored man would scare the rest of the neighborhood they did it. Press Neal, colored, eight miles north of El Dorado, was severely whipped because he said he would vote as he pleased. Sandy Newton, Aaron Cobb (colored), of different townships, were whipped. Monday morning, before daylight, all roads leading to El Dorado were guarded by the militia. They drove all the colored men back; told them to go home and not to come to town that day; if they did they would be killed. Some of them that went by a by-way were shot at; some were visited at their homes and beaten with the guns; some that were in El Dorado were forced to vote the Bourbon ticket. Even some white men were told to go home. About forty colored men went to El Dorado Sunday night for protection. Mr. J. G. Smith, a leading merchant and a reformer in El Dorado, let them stay in his hall over his store. When the Bourbons found it out they went to Smith and told him that if he didn't turn those men out his neck would stretch in five minutes. Smith, thinking it was only a scare, did not pay any attention to it, but the mob sent two more messengers, W.C. Langford and J. C. Wright, to Smith with the same order, "five minutes, or hanging." Smith asked the mob to let the colored men go home unmolested, which they reluctantly agreed to do. Then they told Smith to go home and stay there. The Union Labor party and the reformers did not vote in El Dorado, except one vote for Norwood. A good many colored men have left this county, and more will leave before the year closes. The Bourbons tell the colored men now to come and join their clubs and vote for Cleveland, and they (the colored men) will not be whipped, shot, etc.

These horrible outrages have attracted the attention of the whole country, and in the State of Arkansas the discussion is most bitter. And yet to gain their ends the Democracy stands ready always, either to do or apologize for such action.

If the colored men find comfort and consolation in the outrages on their own people, by the men who have the support and sympathy of these same Mahaska fellows, well and good. If the men under the sharp tooth of the Democratic harrow can have no sympathy from their own people, then indeed have the founts of pity become dried up, and the motives for aid to them become wrecked and sunken in the channels of personal selfishness.

rafe-bird-pooler-1888-03-27.A1:
SHOT DEAD BY A THIEF.
JOSEPH GILL MURDERED ON THE LOUISVILLE ROAD.
Killed While Attempting to Arrest Two Negroes in the Act of Carrying off a Sack of Stolen Beef—The Murderers Escape in the Darkness—An Armed Posse Scouring the Woods for Them and the Police on the Look-out—The Coroner Notified.

Joseph Gill, living at the nine-mile post on the Louisville road, about half a mile this side of Pooler, was shot through the wrist and heart and instantly killed in a woods near Butler's avenue and the six-mile post, half way between the Central railroad and the Louisville road, by an unknown negro at 7 o'clock last night. A load of buckshot was fired into the man's body at short range, killing him instantly.

Yesterday the murdered man discovered that a beef had been slaughtered at the point of the killing. Summoning his brother, Jasper Gill, and Henry Heywood, a hunter, the three went to the place where the beef had been butchered and lay in wait for the thieves. The animal, which belonged to the Widow Farrell, had been butchered and the four quarters put in sacks.

Jasper Gill and Heywood were posted not far distant, while Joseph Gill remained near the sacks which contained the beef. Shortly after night fall three negroes came up, and without seeing Joseph Gill they reached down to take hold of the sacks.

"DROP THAT BEEF."

Gill arose from his place of concealment, and called out loud enough for his brother Jasper and Heywood to hear him, "drop that beef."

One of the negroes, who was only a few feet away, emptied the contents of a shotgun into Gill's breast, killing him instantly, and then all three of the negroes ran. Jasper Gill and Heywood were so taken by surprise as they saw Joseph Gill fall, that they did not fire at the fugitives, but hurried to the spot to book after their companion. They found him dead.

He was taken home and the neighborhood aroused. All Pooler turned out to hunt the murderer, Benjamin Rothwell, postmaster, and J. B. Forehand armed themselves, caught the 10:10 o'clock freight train and hurried to Savannah and telephoned Sergt. Killourhy from the depot as soon as the train arrived. The message was received at the barracks at 12:15 this morning, in time to
to Savannah and telephoned Sergt. Killourhy from the depot as soon as the train arrived. The message was received at the barracks at 12:15 this morning, in time to instruct the second night relief of police to watch all avenues, as it was expected that the murderers would try to steal into the city. The Ocean Steamship police were also instructed to vigilantly guard the river front.

Coroner Dixon was notified of the murder by telephone, and Messrs. Rothwell and Forehand notified Sheriff Ronan and Detective Wetherhorn at 1 o'clock this morning.

HUNTING THE MURDERER.

Over twenty men were scouring the woods last night in the vicinity of Pooler, and while suspicion does not rest on any particular party, it is not thought possible that the murderer and his accomplices can escape.

The police will carefully note what negros are missing from the market this morning.

The murdered man was about 27 years of age, and leaves a wife but no children. He has taken an active part in apprehending thieves, and about a year ago arrested a negro for stealing an ox from Mr. Rothwell, and the thief was sent to the penitentiary for two years.

THE MURDERED MAN.

The deceased is spoken of very highly as an industrious man, fearless in the face of danger and commanding the respect of all who knew him. If his murderers are found by the indignant citizens who are now on the lookout for them it is hardly possible that the county will ever be put to the expense of trying them.

If they are not apprehended by daylight blood hounds will be put upon their trail, and they will be hunted down from the place where the murder was committed.
rafe-bird-pooler-1888-03-27.A2:
GILL'S SLAYER AT LARGE.
The Coroner's Investigation of the Shooting at Six-Mile-Post.
Shooting at Six-Mile-Post.

The slayer of Joseph Gill at the six-mile-post on the Louisville road is still at large. Coroner Dixon held an inquest over the remains of the murdered man yesterday. Gill's two brothers, F. M. Gill and Jasper Gill, testified to the shooting as detailed by the MORNING News. They could not identify the thieves or say whether they were white or black. F. M. Gill said that his posse pursued the thieves, firing at them as they ran away.

"Rafe" Bird (colored) testified to seeing two suspicious negroes Friday afternoon, one of whom had a musket. He thinks they were butchers, and he testified that after the shooting of Gill a musket was found near the beef, and he thought it was the one he had seen the negro have during the afternoon. He would know them, he said, if he should see them again.

John Graham who was left by F. M. Gill to watch the beef until he could collect a posse, swore that while he was watching the beef a man came up with a pistol in his hand, examined the sacks containing the meat and went off.

The only new feature in the examination not covered by the Morning News report yesterday was the finding of a hatchet, butcher-knife and butcher's steel, which was omitted by request of those having the search for the murderers in charge, and the fact that Gill's brother and Mr. Haywood pursued the thieves and fired on them.

The verdict of the jury was: "We find that Joseph Gill came to his death from a gunshot wound at the hands of some party or parties unknown to the jury, and we consider it murder."

Somebody must be killed from the holling that is going on.’ My wife said, ‘Bird, don’t go; you might get shot yourself.’ Henry Marcus, Sam and myself all went in the direction of the shooting, where we met the posse. I hailed them 100 yards off and said, ‘Who’s dat?’ Mr. Marion Gill caught my voice, and said, ‘Rafe, my brother’s got killed; for God’s sake come and help me.’ All the rest of the posse broke and run. They thought we had guns, and they said they ran to load their guns, because their’s were empty.

“I never killed the beef, and know nothing of it. At 5 o’clock that evening Marcus came home from Parnell’s, where he had been at work, and none of us left the house until we heard the firing. I got up about 5 o’clock that morning, woke Henry and then my wife. I heard the train go by at 6 o’clock and fix the time by that. Shortly after, and without breakfast, my wife and me left home and went to Marion Gill’s and got there about a little after 7. I stayed at Marion Gill’s that afternoon till 1 o’clock, my wife and me butheering fifty head of chickens. Martha Roberts, my next door neighbor, who lives about half of a quarter of a mile from my house, and an old colored woman named Rose knows this statement to be true.”

Bird then went on to detail his visit to Savannah on Saturday and his staying here Sunday, Monday and Tuesday forenoon looking for the two men that he had met on the railroad, so that he could point them out to Detective Wetherhorn, and concluded his statement, in a flood of tears, as to how he had been treated by his captors Tuesday night.

TIED BY HIS THUMBS.

“When they arrested me,” he said, “they took me to station No. 1, on the Central railroad, and tried to get me to tell them about the shooting. I told them I did not know any more than I had told the Coroner. They then took me about 100 yards back of the warehouse and tied my thumbs together and threatened to hang me up by them half an hour at a time until I did tell. I said, ‘Gentlemen, I know nothing about the shooting. I can’t tell any more than I done to you. I didn’t kill the beef.’ They then took me back to the warehouse, where they kept me until very late. It must been long about midnight. It was a good while after the 9 o'clock train passed. They then carried me about a mile out in the swamp, in the woods, and said they was going to lynch me. I begged them and prayed to them all I knew how not to lynch me, and when I saw they were going to kill me, I said, to save my life, I knowed I could show them a man that killed the beef. That it was a colored man named Brown, who lived at the 4-mile hill. They then went and arrested him and carried him to the station. But they let him go for when it come daylight I told them better; that I had been compelled to lie on somebody to save my life."

Further developments in the Gill murder will be awaited with interest, and that the guilty parties are spotted by Detective Wetherhorn seems to be pretty generally believed. There was a rumor that Marcus had been arrested yesterday afternoon, but he is still at large.

All this, and the finding of the liver, was to the detective strong circumstantial evidence pointing to a full knowledge of Bird not only about the killing of the beef, but the killing of Joseph Gill.

SUSPICIONS AGAINST BIRD.

It was also suspicious that Marcus, who had so long laid around Bird's house, where there was little or nothing to eat, should leave Sunday when the liver and heart of the beef had evidently been taken to Bird's cabin, and the head and tripe of the beef had been given to Bird for carrying the beef out of the swamp after the killing of Gill.

Detective Wetherhorn says that while he has been keeping a sharp lookout for Marcus, and heard of him being in town Monay, he has thus far been unable to lay dands on him, but that he has such a perfect description of the fellow that he cannot well elude the vigilance of those who are watching for him. Mr. Wetherhorn expects more developments to-day, and it is likely that Sam Bird, the boy, and others, will be put under surveillance, and possibly under arrest to-day.

THE PRISONER'S STORY.

A MORNING NEWS reporter interviewed Bird in his cell at the jail last night. The negro adheres to his statement given before the Coroner's jury, and in concluding the interview where he detailed his experience in the swamp when he was threatened with being lynched, he broke down and wept copiously. He is tall and very black, a type of the thriftless and slovenly negro that is content with wearing cast off clothing, and he is evidently a stranger to daily ablutions. His hair is extremely short even for a negro, and he wears a scattered beard and moustache, both of which are as kinky as the wool on his head. His eyes are neither lacking in luster nor are they bright, but there is a shrewdness lurking in them, although the pupils are large and neither retreating nor staring. He speaks with more than ordinary care and with an intelligent approach to frankness; his phraseology is not a continuation of the African dialect, although he drops into it occasionally as if he would like to be considered more ignorant than he really is. He made the following statement:

BIRD'S STATEMENT.

"My name is Rafe Bird. I was born in Liberty county, and was last owned by Jacob Wise, in Bryan county. My occupation is daily labor. I was married twenty years ago in Bryan county to Hannah Sheftall. We have had thirteen children, eight of whom are dead. We moved to Savannah after the big August storm, in September. I worked here on and off; first for Smith & Kelly, and afterward at draying on the Bay. I worked for Mr. McCormick. Mr. Goodwin, Mr. Heidt and others, off and on. I quit draying fall before last, at which time I was working for Mr. McCormick. I went out into the country, moving to the race track on the Louisville road, and went to farming. I farmed there in 1886. I next moved to the Widow Jones place, five miles from Savannah, on the Louisville road, and farmed there in 1887. This year, in January, I moved to the seven mile post, on the Louisville road, on Mr. Henry Jackson's land, renting a part of the tract to farm it and raise rice, sugar cane, peas and whatever else I could grow.

THE STORY OF HIS ARREST.

I was arrested Tuesday evening about 5 o'clock by Mr. Marion Gill and Ben Rothwell, ticket agent at No. 1, on the Central road. I was at home sitting in the door. Mr. Joe Ferrill was a little ways off with a gun and Jack Gill held the horses. Mr. Rothwell told me that he had a warrant for me and to consider myself under arrest. Then Gill collared me and took me behind the house, and Mr. Ferrill tied me. I made no resistance. I told them that I had never had anything to do with killing the beef and knew nothing about it. That is true. I never even brought any beef to market. I had helped to tote the beef out of the swamp, and I helped tote Joe Gill's body out of the swamp to my house, where it was laid out until the wagon came for it. We did not go to bed that night but Henry Marcus and I slept some sitting in our chairs.

"The beef was killed between my house and the railroad. My house is about one half a mile from the railroad track, and it was about one half mile from my house to where the beef was. I did not see any one go out to watch the beef.

BEEN HUNTING STRAY CATTLE.

"I had been out that afternoon looking for five head of cattle that I had in the swamp. I walked in the direction of the railroad, thinking that as they had not shown up for some four days, that they had been turned over by the railroad. When I reached the railroad, and had walked a
railroad, thinking that as they had not shown up for some four days, that they had been turned over by the railroad. When I reached the railroad, and had walked a short distance, I saw two colored men on the track. One was leaning on a musket and the other was standing by him talking. I was faced toward Savannah, and they were behind me about twenty steps, facing the same way. I knew their faces and recognized them as belonging in Savannah, but I could not recall their names. I said: 'Hello! what are you doing up here? They started toward me, and when they came up they said, 'Pardner what are you doing up here? I said: 'I see staying up here now. Business was too dull in town to make a living. I am up here trying to farm.' It is not strange that I should not remember their names, for I have met two or three men in jail to-day whom I knew and who knew me, and we had to ask each other our names. It was about 2:30 o'clock when I met the two men on the railroad. I told them that I was looking for some yearlings that had been gone some four days, and asked them if they had seen any knocked off by the road. They said they had not. I asked them where they had been, and where they were going.

THE STORY OF THE TWO STRANGERS.

"They said they were going to Savannah. They said that they had been up the road to a turpentine camp where they had been offered $1 per day if they would come up, but when they got there they found differently, and were on their way back home. They had stalled all night Thursday night, they said, at Whitesville, and had been in Dan Martin's turpentine camp, but they did not give the name of the turpentine camp up the road. As we walked along they were a little behind me, part of the time talking to me, and part of the time talking low to themselves. After we had gone about a mile I turned off and took the dirt road and saw no mors of them.

"After walking about a quarter of a mile an the dirt road, or Louisville road, I met Joe Ferrill coming down in a gallop and I stopped him. Ferrill and Marion Gill had agreed to buy a yearling from me, and I was to furnish it, if I could find it, in time to butcher it Friday evening for Saturday's
rafe-bird-pooler-1888-03-27.A5:
BIRD IN THE LAW'S NET.
THE SUPPOSED SLAYER OF JOE GILL BEHIND THE BARS.
Mile Post—A Pooler Posse's Midnight Ride to the Swamp with the Prisoner—His Narrow Escape from Lynching—Bird Tells the Story of His Arrest and Denies the Shooting—Marcus, His Suspected Accomplice, Still at Large.

It begins to look as if there is to be an early solution of the Gill murder mystery. The arrest of Rafe Bird (colored) yesterday morning is the first step in that direction.

Some time last Friday a beef belonging to the Widow Ferrill, daughter of Marion Gill, was found butchered and hidden behind a log in the swamps near Butler avenue, about half way between the Central railroad and the Louisville road, near Pooler. From the best information obtainable Marion Gill had disposed of some cows to Bird, but as the latter had failed to pay for the stock, Marion Gill had agreed with Bird that he would take yearlings in payment. Bird was to bring him a yearling that morning in time to be butchered for market Saturday morning. Instead of doing so Bird and his wife went to Gill's Friday morning, where they killed a lot of chickens for Gill, and where Bird reported that he could not find the yearlings. Gill insisted that he should go out in the woods and hunt them up, but Bird kept making excuses, and finally Gill sent his son to look up his own cattle, and incidentally to keep a lookout for Bird's yearlings. The son discovered the butchered beef in the woods and reported the facts to his father.

SUSPICION RESTED ON BIRD.

Suspicion was at once directed toward Bird by reason of the fact that he had shown no disposition to look for the cattle, but in the later and more exciting incidents of the evening, the suspicion seems to have been dropped.

The readers of the MORNING NEWS are familiar with the facts connected with the Friday night tragedy, when the Gill brothers, Haywood, and their posse took up their station to watch the beef and catch the thief, and how Joseph Gill was shot down.

Detective Wetherhorn at first declined to lend his services and aid in tracking the murderer, but finding that no one seemed inclined to aid in bringing the guilty parties to justice he consented, on a second interview, to do all in his power.

After a full consultation with the citizens of Pooler and with the relatives of the dead
ties to justice he consented, on a second interview, to do all in his power.

After a full consultation with the citizens of Pooler and with the relatives of the dead man he suggested that Bird be sent down to Savannah. The negro had testified before the Coroner's jury to meeting two men Friday afternoon on the railroad track, one of whom had a musket, which he identified as the one found on Saturday in the neighborhood of where the shooting occurred. His statement was to the effect that while he could not recall the names of the two men, he had worked with them in Savannah when he was in the employ of Mr. Andrew McCormick, and he could readily recognize them.

BIRD'S CONFLICTING STORIES.

On Sunday Gill brought Bird to the city and turned him over to Detective Wetherhorn. But Mr. Wetherhorn found Bird's stories conflicting. His description of the two negroes varied in essential details, and the detective soon discovered by carefully watching that Bird was making no sincere effort to find anyone. It was found, too, by the detective that Bird had only been employed three days by Mr. McCormick, although he had created the impression that he had been in his employ for some time. Mr. Wetherhorn found Mr. John Downing, who keeps the time of the hands, and the names of all the men employed when Bird was working for Mr. McCormick were called over in Bird's presence, and while he had said he could not remember the names of either of the two men he saw without hearing their names called he was unable to fix upon any of those on the time book. In fact his conduct was so suspicious that the suggestion was then made to the detective that Bird should be placed under arrest.

On Sunday and Monday Mr. Wetherhorn pretty thoroughly convinced himself that Bird was not trying to find any one. In a consultation Monday evening Mr. Wetherhorn learned that when the butchered beef was found the liver and heart were missing. He was convinced that whoever killed the beef would not take those parts to Savannah, and that they must have been taken to some contiguous cabin for a morning meal. Reasoning on this train, what cabin more probable than the Bird cabin. It was near the scene of the killing. Bird himself had intimated to him that some one might think he was connected with it as it happened so near his house. There was no corroboration of Bird's story of meeting two men, one of whom had a musket.

A STRANGE COINCIDENCE.

It was also a strange coincidence that Bird had found the musket on Saturday. It was suspicious, too, that almost immediately after Joe Gill was shot, Bird, his 12-year-old boy Sam and Henry Marcus, a worthless negro who had been hanging about Bird's place, should come upon the scene and make themselves known, Bird hallooing out not to shoot, that it was him. Putting all these things together, Detective Wetherhorn told the Pooler folks to go back home; that he would keep Bird in town until Tuesday noon, and that they should use their judgment and try to learn from Bird's children if they had had liver on the table recently. The Birds had been living in great penury, and to that degree that they had been known to cook and eat the entrails of the chickees butchered for Marion Gill.

On Tuesday Mrs. Ferrill made an excuse to visit the Bird cabin, taking with her a basket of provisions. Gaining the confidence of a 10-year-old girl of Bird's, she very artlessly told that they had liver to eat, as did old "Rose," an aged negress who made her home at Bird's, but the boy Sam, a lad of 12, seemed to have been posted, and he denied any knowledge of having liver in the house for over a year.

FINDING THE BEEF'S LIVER.

When Mrs. Ferrill communicated this intelligence to her father and supplemented it by saying that as she was coming away from the house she had met Bird returning, Marion Gill, Ben Rothwell, Joseph Ferrill, and Jack Gill mounted their horses and galloped over to the Bird cabin. Bird was immediately taken into custody at about 5 o'clock Tuesday afternoon, and a search of the house resulted in finding a portion of the beef liver in a wash boiler.

Bird was tied and taken to the railroad station, and an effort was made to get him to tell all that he knew about the affair, but he persisted in his original story, with slight variations. Later in the night a larger body of men, armed, made a descent upon the guards, and taking him to the swamp threatened to lynch him if he did not tell the truth. He then criminated a negro
rafe-bird-pooler-1888-03-27.A7:
sack that had one of the quarters of beef in it.

Those who examined the beef say that the heart, liver and lights were not with the beef when they found it concealed Friday morning. It is a custom to put the tripe, head, liver, heart and lights in one sack, and the last three articles were not in the sack with the head. Bird's wife denied that Henry Marcus had any clothing there except a worthless pair of pantalons, although Bird told Wetherhorn that Marcus had gone back Monday to his (Bird's) house for his clothing. Bird's wife says Marcus has never been back but is running on the steamer Ethel. She wanted to come down to Savannah yesterday, and Sam, the boy who is in Marion Gill's charge, was permitted to take a message to a friend of Bird's wife, whom she wanted to come down with her, but he pointedly refused and she did not come.

BROWN NO. 2 AGAIN.

Yesterday morning Brown issued from his concealment, and under the protection of the gray headed old minister came to town, where they waited long and patiently in the office of Justice Warring Russell, Jr., for Detective Wetherhorn. But 12 o'clock and 1 o'clock came, and no Wetherhorn. The old preacher could wait no longer, but told Brown to remain, and he left for home. Later in the afternoon the detective returned to the city, and while pretty well satisfied before, he had no doubt that Brown No. 2 was an innocent man and he was permitted to return home.

Marcus is still at large. He is evidently living very low, awaiting developments. Detective Wetherhorn, in an interview with a MORNING NEWS reporter last evening, said that his Wednesday night experience, which included an extra thirty mile drive he had not calculated upon, had so thoroughly tired him out that he was going to rest last night, but that every effort would be made to apprehend Marcus. It was evident to him that Marcus was a thriftless, lazy negro. He had laid out in an open shed at Bird's house, where there was little or nothing but corn bread and chicken entrails to eat, and it was suspicious that when there was plenty in the house to eat, with no talk of arresting Bird, that he should suddenly disappear Sunday, and hide away.

BIRD'S BAD CHARACTER.

The character of Bird, the detective says, is bad. He is an indolent negro, and while Marion Gill had done a great deal for him and let him have the cattle he had never paid for them and never made an effort to pay for them. It was strange, too, that Bird should never mention what Bird's wife had told him.

Bird's wife told the officer yesterday that she heard a shot Friday morning before she and her husband started to Marion Gill's, and that she had said to her old man, "Did you hear dat shot? I wouldn't be sprised ef dat wasn't one of yoh veahlins dun got shot out dah in de swamp." Bird has never made any mention of such an occurrence. When the detective asked her why Bird had not gone out there to see about it, she said they were in too big a hurry to get over to Mr. Marion Gill's to get to work. But the distance from Bird's to Marion Gill's is not over a mile and a half, and Bird's statement is to the effect that he got up at 5 o'clock that morning, woke his wife up and they left for Marion Gill's without their breakfast, right after the 6 o'clock train passed, getting to Gill's after 7 o'clock. The detective says that when he asked her why she did not send Sam to see about the yearling, she replied she never thought of it. The detective's theory is that they had liver for breakfast that morning, and the heart and lights have never yet been discovered.

Detective Wetherhorn says that he feels satisfied that Bird knows all about the affair, and that at one time he was about to make a clean breast of it. That was on Wednesday last, when Marion Gill feelingly alluded to the many charitable and kindly deeds he had done for Bird; that he did not accuse him of shooting his brother; that he did not care for the beef, but that he did want to know who was the slayer of his brother, and he appealed to Bird to tell him what he knew about it.

MOVED BY GILL'S APPEAL.

The appeal seemed to touch Bird, who sat with his head bent, and at the conclusion of Mr. Gill's impassioned pleading for the truth Bird raised his head, and acknowledging the kindness of Marion Gill, started to say, "Till tell you all I know about it," hesitated, looked around at those about him, and then changing his demeanor, said that he knew nothing beyond that which he had already told. His statement made for publication in the MORNING NEWS of yesterday is all that Rafe Bird has had to say since the tragedy with which so many connect him as an accomplice.
Bird, Detective Weterhorn says, got into trouble in Bryan county, where he kept a doggery, and the officers came down nere after him some years ago and took him up there. Bird says that he was indicted for selling liquor without giving bond, and that he got out of it by paying a couple of lawyers $25.
The relatives and friends of the murdered man have relaxed none of their vigilance and are watching every suspicious movement, both in the vicinity of Pooler and in this city, and that Bird's neck was saved in the swamp Tuesday night is due to the presence of mind and considerate judgment of Mr. Haywood, to whom the enraged posse listened, although after finding the liver in Bird's cabin they felt sure they had the right man.

THE GILL MURDER CASE.
The Pooler Tragedy as Much of A Mystery as Ever. It begins to look if the murderer or
The Pooler Tragedy as Much of A Mystery as Ever.

It begins to look as if the murderer or murderers of Joe Gill have thoroughly succeeded in hiding their tracks. The circumstances of the murder are still fresh in the public mind. Some thief or thieves killed a beef in the neighborhood of Joseph Gill's house near Pooler in April last, and the beef was found concealed near the spot where it was butchered during the day. At nightfall Joe Gill, his brother, and a posse took up their station in proximity to the beef to confront and take into custody the thieves. When they approached Joe Gill came forward from his hiding place and accosted the thieves, when he was shot down, his murderer escaping in the darkness.

Detective Wetherhorn, after two days' investigation of all the surrounding circumstances, arrested Rafe Bird, a negro living near the scene of the murder, and last month Detective Hanley arrested Abram Edy (colored) on the charge of the murder. The grand jury of the superior court, on Wednesday last, after an inquiry, failed to indict either of them, and they have been discharged.

While it has never been thought that Bird was a party to the killing, he was suspected of knowing who killed the beef, and certain suspicious acts on the day of and the day following the murder led to his arrest. It was shown that Bird and his wife did not go to their work the morning of the day the beef was killed as early as was their custom; that Bird was in the habit of going to his work with one Mathis, a negro who was staying with him, and that on the morning of the day the beef was killed he sent Mathis on ahead. That it was the custom of Bird to take his boy with him when he went to work, but on that morning he left the boy at home.

Mathis was arrested by Detective Wetherhorn, but his conduct was so clearly disingenuous that no suspicion attached to him, and he was never committed to jail. He did deepen the suspicion against Bird, however, by relating the incident of two visits from unknown men to Bird's cabin the night of the murder after the body of Joe Gill had been removed to his home near Poolers, and after the excitement had in a measure subsided. It was also learned that the liver of the beef had furnished a meal for the Bird family, and a portion of it was found hidden away in Bird's cabin. Evidence was not waiting to prove that
the liver of the beef had furnished a meal for the Bird family, and a portion of it was found hidden away in Bird's cabin. Evidence was not wanting to prove that when the beef was removed to Bird's cabin after the killing of Gill there was no liver in the sacks containing the beef.

Bird's statements were contradictory, and he claimed that during the afternoon of the day the beef was killed he met two negroes on the railroad near the scene of the killing, one of whom had a musket, and with whom he had worked in Savannah for some time, and whom he claimed he could identify if brought to Savannah. He was brought to the city and the pay roll of the firm he claimed to have been employed by did not corroborate his statement as to the length of time employed, and a close watch on his actions established the fact that he was making no effort to find the two negroes whom he claimed to have met. Further than this it was shown that he had told Mathis in the market that if he could get away he would go further south, or over into Mississippi.

In the light of all these circumstances there was a strong suspicion against him. When the liver was found concealed in his cabin the enraged citizens of Poor took Bird to the swamps, and by threats led him to criminalize one Brown, a negro living some miles further up the road. Brown had no trouble in satisfying his captors that he was not in the neighborhood of the crime and he was released by the posse, Bird taking his statement back when brought out of the swamp and confronted by Brown. Bird was then brought to jail in this city, where he has been kept in confinement until the grand jury this week returned "no bill," and Bird was released from custody.

Another suspicious fact connected with the case was that on the morning following the night of the murder, Bird told Mathis where to look and he would find a gun, which Mathis did, and found the musket which had been fired with fatal aim full in the breast of Joseph Gill.

The theory that Bird knew who killed the beef, that two visits from strange persons had been paid to Bird's cabin, and without inviting them in, but to better conceal their identity from Mathis he had gone to the door and talked in a low tone to one of the visitors, and had gone down the road a part of the way with the other visitor or visitors, all led to the natural conclusion that he knew more of the circumstances than he was inclined to furnish.

Whether the case will rest here depends upon the course which the authorities take in the matter. It is strange that the gun, the hatchet, the canes and the steel found in one of the sacks have never been traced to an owner, although the musket has initials cut deeply in the stock. The rewards offered for the identification and apprehension of the murderer will no doubt stimulate the detectives to renewed effort to track down the guilty man.

Last Monday morning a quarrel begun between Steve Allen, a colored man, and Mr. Hodnett, section boss on the railroad just above Oxford, which resulted in the killing of Hodnett by Allen in what appears to have been in the most unprovoked manner. It seems the quarrel began about fifteen cents. Allen was one of the hands in the employ of the railroad and was working under Hodnett. From what we learn Allen cursed Hodnett who thereupon discharged Allen from his service. This so enraged the negro he threatened to kill Hodnett in consequence of which Hodnett obtained a shot-gun in town with which as he is reported to have told Morr. w & Loudie that he wanted to protect himself against the negro who he was atraid would carry out his threat. Hodnett went back to the railroad and a he was approaching the hands at work was shot by Allen who was posted on top of the cut.

Monday night in consequence of the belief that Allen waylaid Hod nett and killed him without any demonstration whatever from Hod nett, a crowd gathered around the jail at Oxford with the view of lynching the negro. But the Shér iff had removed the negro to safer quarters.

We would not do injustice to a negro if we could avoid it and in giving the facts of the matter we give that most current in the community without being able to write positively of the true state of the case. It is not known who the would-be lynchers were but it is reported that a train brought some men here from Water Valley. There is danger in lynch law but if Allen wayland Hodnett and was moved to his course by revenge so unjustifiable, no doubt the parties seeking vengeance on him felt justifiable for the attempted lynching.
steve-allen-oxford-1888-07-02.A2: As a failure the attempted lyching last Monday night took the cake. The negro is about the only one rejoicing over the failure.
steve-allen-oxford-1888-07-02.A3: Quite a ripple of excitement occurred in our city on Friday evening over the report that Steve Allen the negro who killed the section master at Oxford was lodged in our jail for safe keeping. Telegraphic communication was opened up with Water Valley where a mob was organized to proceed to this place immediately. The report was however soon proven to be false and all was quiet again. The people seem to be determined to lynch this murderer wherever they can find him. The sheriff has so far kept him concealed from them.—Holly Springs South

Topics of the Times Given in a Terse and Spicy Manner.

The miners' strike in the Lehigh valley has been declared off.

At Wichita, Kas., John Smith shot and killed Sam Brock in a dive.

David Shields, an Attica, Ind., tailor committed suicide at Danville by taking laudanum.

Six men were arrested at Nicholasville, Ky., charged with robbing Greenbaum's distillery of whisky.

Grant Porter and John Burkel, colored prisoners in the Athens, O., jail, overpowered the sheriff and escaped.

Officer Wright was shot and mortally wounded while in pursuit of an escaped criminal at Chesapeake, Mo.

The crumbling skeleton of a man encased in a decayed barrel, ten feet under ground, was dug up at Pueblo, Col.

Robert Lincoln has written a letter again refusing to allow his name to be used in connection with any political office.

In a fight with small gloves, in Cincinnati, Sunday, between Johnnie O'Brien and Joe Kilroy, the latter was knocked out in the ninth round.

A young English student named Parkings, who jumped from the fourth story of the burning university at Mitchell, Dak., died from his injuries.

Mary Reilly, a little girl at Westchester, N. Y., bitten by a mad dog, began to bark and snap, gnashed her teeth and died after two days' agony.

Widow of the murdered Chicago millionaire, Amos J. Snell, has offered $10,000 reward for the arrest of W. B. Tascott, his supposed murderer.

Governor Lowry, of Mississippi, is guilty of a misdemeaner under the state law for accepting railway passes. He has not, however, been arrested.

A passenger train on the Erie road jumped the track at Scio, N. Y., Sunday morning, killing one passenger and maiming twelve others, of whom four will die.

A. C. Myers and Frank West, of Durango, Col., were arrested and taken to Kansas, charged with the murder of Archibald Douglass, at Lyons, Kas., twelve years ago.

The Boston stock exchange has decided to prohibit members from dealing with bucket shops under penalty of $1,000 for the first offense, and expulsion for the second offense.

At Tyrone, Pa., Charles W. Stettler, while drunk, shot and seriously wounded Landlord D. H. Hazen, of the Arlington hotel, and then attempted suicide by cutting his throat with a pen knife.

An American posse of officers pursuing the Stein passenger train robbers from Arizona into Mexico, were thrown into a dungeon at Janos, Chihauhua. The people along the border are ablaze over the arrest.

Judge E. C. Ruggles, a family man of Wichita, Kan., skipped with his lady stenographer, having mortgaged or sold his property for sums aggregating probably $75,000. A reward of $1,000 is offered for the judge.

The chairman of the National committee of the Union Labor party has issued a call for a National convention to be held at Cincinnati, May 15, to nominate candidates for president and vice president of the United States.

Fair girls and spectacled mothers at Trenton, Ga., overpowered the sheriff, dragged negro Tom Roof from jail and vindicated the honor of Mrs. Joe Morrison and the female sex, by fatally swinging him from a shed rafter.

Lynched by Women. TRENTON, Ga., March 12.—Tom Roof, the negro arrested in Chattanooga on Thursday for assaulting Mrs. Joe Morrison, at this place, was taken from the jail Saturday night and hanged from a rafter of the shed in the public square. Sheriff Bird resisted the mob to the last, but he was overpowered, and was compelled to surrender the keys of the jail. Roof confessed the crime just before he was lynched. The mob consisted mostly of women. The Brussels Burns at Her Wharf. SAN FRANCISCO, March 12.—The British bark Brussels burned at her wharf yesterday morning. The loss is $60,000. She was about to start for Havre. VICTIMS OF A FIRE.
Six Lives Lost by the Burning of a Springfield (Mass.) Newspaper Office—As Many More Injured—Hemmed in by the Flames the Unfortunates Leap from a Fifth-Story Window.

SPEINGFIELD, Mass., March 8.—The new office of the Evening Union at the corner of Main and Worthington streets was burned about 4 o'clock yesterday afternoon, and the blaze was attended with the most sickening horror, six of the employes meeting a terrible death, most of them jumping from the fifth story and being crushed into a shapeless mass below. Six others were badly injured. The fire was first discovered in the mailing-room and clouds of smoke were pouring out of the lower-story windows before the fifty souls on the upper floor were aware of their danger.

The unfortunate men and women who crowded into the editorial-rooms met a horrible fate. Some were cut off in the composing-room and more are believed to have perished, as several fell back into the flames. The employes who rushed into the editorial-rooms were cut off from the escape in the rear and had to face the horrible alternative of burning to death or jumping to the sidewalk below.

The fire department responded promptly, but it seemed an age before it reached the windows on the fifth floor. A ladder was put to the fourth story, and the sight of rescue so near seemed to madden the suffering group at the two windows, who dropped in succession to the sidewalk below. Six fell in this way, some of them being forced out and some madly leaping. The crowd groaned and turned their heads away as the victims whirled through the air. The killed are:

Henry I. Goulding, foreman of the Union composing-room, burned to death; Miss G. Thompson, proof-reader; Mrs. Frederick E. Farley, editorial department, fell from the window; Mr. Lamzon, of Quebec, jumped to the sidewalk; W. E. Hovey, of Boston, fell to the sidewalk and was crushed; Mr. Brown, a compositor.

Joseph Landford was standing on the sidewalk at the end of the building farthest from the corner when Mrs. Farley fell. He stood his ground and reached out his arms to catch her. She fell on his neck, throwing him to the ground senseless. Mrs. Farley was killed instantly. Mr. Landford was soon restored to consciousness and is not seriously hurt. The terrible experience of those in the window is told by Mr. Hill, the managing editor. He was in the news-room when he heard the news of the fire. Hill ran out and told the men and women to stent for the roof in the rear, and many of them did so. He felt perfectly safe for a few minutes, as he saw the men climbing over the roof, near the old quarters of the office. Fifteen of the employes, however, rushed to the front six of them going into the room of News Editor Shipley, on the corner. Hill opened the window and shouted: "For God's sake put up a ladder." The crowd below looked dazed. He took off his coat and threw it. He picked up books and files of the paper and hurled them out to attract attention. The smoke became dense and he could not breath.

The ladder started and seemed to creep up the side of the building. Mrs. Farley saw the ladder and frantically jumped for it. She seemed to roll down the plane and struck on the walk in a heen. The copy-holder started to follow. Mr. Hill caught her by the waist and held her fast.

The crowd tried to shout words of encouragement. The ladder seemed frozen to the post. A wave of flame shot through the window, singing Hill's hair and clothes. The ladder had come at last, and the copy-holder, who had struggled in his arms, caught it. The crowd was breathless. The hiss of the first stream of water was the only sound. She grasped the rounds firmly and went down safely.

"Go ahead," Hill said; "I can wait." The rest of the group went down, sliding and tumbling over the rounds, but reached the ground safely. Hill finally swung himself under the ladder and made his descent, with another man in front.

The building belonged to E. Wight. The Union editorial and composing-rooms occupied the entire fifth floor. The counting-room was on the first floor. The press-room and mailing-rooms were in the basement. The total loss is about $40,000.

CHARLES PARKHUEST, aged twelve years, while fooling with a gun on the 8th near Attica, Kan., shot and killed Charles Sleepy and fatally wounded George Sleepy.

DEMOCRATS of Indiana will hold their State convention in Indianapolis April 23 to elect delegates to the National convention.

ONE of the buildings of the Williamson County (Tenn.) poor-house was burned on the 8th, and William Johnson and Dora Shannon (colored), both insane, perished in the flames.

On the 8th the Mississippi Legislature adjourned sine dis.

A FIRE on the 9th at Harrisburg, Ill., destroyed eleven business houses and five dwellings.

THE Methodist University building at Mitchell, D. T., was burned on the 9th, and out of forty inmates ten were badly injured, one having died, while others were thought to be fatally hurt.

Five men and four women committed suicide in Chicago during the seven days ended on the 9th, and three other persons failed in their attempts to take their lives.

In the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy strike there was no change on the 9th. In Judge Gresham's court in Chicago action on the petition of the Burlington Company for an order compelling the Wabash road to transport and deliver cars tendered by the Burlington was postponed until the 12th. In Omaha Judge Dundy issued an order enjoining the Union Pacific Railroad Company and its engineers from refusing to perform their duties under the Inter-State Commerce law and enjoining the engineers from organizing or combining to direct any strike.

At Emmetttsburg, Ia., the veterinary stable of Dr. Hayes was burned on the 9th, and several valuable horses were lost.

On the 9th the Illinois League of Republican clubs was organized at Springfield, with William W. Tracy, of that city, as president.

FIVE Italian counterfeiters were captured on the 9th at Norfolk, Va. They had flooded the city with silver counterfeit dollars.

MACEY WARNER was hanged on the 9th at Jeffersonville, Ind., for the murder, April 15, 1887, of Frank Harris.

A negro named Tom Roof, who assaulted Mrs. Morrison in Trenton, Ga., was taken from jail on the 10th and lynched by a mob of women.

On the 10th Mrs. Henrietta Snell, of Chicago, widow of Amos J. Snell, the murdered millionaire, offered a reward of $10,000 for the arrest of William B. Tuscott, the supposed murderer.

A hail-storm on the 10th along the Mississippi coast caused ruin to the vegetables, growing fruit, etc.

It looked on the 10th as if the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy strike was nearing an end, and rumors were current that the strikers were anxious to return to work. The fact that the Brotherhood was unable to control competing roads had been disastrous.

The Legislature of Utah adjourned sine die on the 10th. All the old bills designed to protect the polygamists and aid them in fighting the United States laws heretofore passed and vetoed by Governor Murray were again passed at this session and vetoed by Governor West.

Rudolph Heller's wife and child were suffocated by natural gas on the 12th at Finlay, O.

The Chicago, Burlington & Quincy rail way strike as regards the prospects of its extension to other roads was in abeyance on the 12th pending Judge Gresham's decision in the Wabash case. The arguments had been concluded and the case taken under advisement.

The Legislature of Wyoming adjourned sine die on the 12th.

Mormon elders who had been making converts in small districts of Botecourt County, Va., were notified on the 12th to leave or be lynched.

Near Mason City, Ia., the family of H. L. Brown, nine in all, were taken violently sick at supper on the 11th, and Mr. Brown and one child had died. How their food was poisoned had not been discovered.

A fire destroyed the works of the Grand Detour Plow Company at Dixon, Ill., on the 12th, causing a loss of over $100,000.

LOUISVILLE, April 22.—At Mouse Tail Landing, on the Tennessee river, near Paducah, one Ward, on Saturday, shot J. Stafford. Ward, it is alleged, had been circulating disrespectful stories about Stafford's daughter. Stafford found him in a crowd at the landing and at the pistol's point compelled him to confess he had lied. He went immediately home and returned with a shotgun, just as Stafford was mounting his horse, and shot him dead without warning. The Missouri Rising.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., April 22.—[Special Telegram to the BEE.]—The Missouri river is rising again here. The banks on both sides are being cut out. The house on the island, which has withstood several floods, is carried away.

MACON, Mo., April 22.—[Special Telegram to the BEE.]—John Lutz, who resides at Clinton, Ia., fell dead in the depot while waiting for the Hannibal train to go home. Cause, heart disease.

TREADWELL ACQUITTED.
The Southern Kansas Cattle King Declared to be Justifiad in Killing Clarke.
John Holmes, of La Plata, Acquitted of Attempted Murder-A Deadbeat Vacates Omaha.
A Killing on the Tennessee River With a Rumored Lynching—Matricide in Iowa.
ANTHONY, Kan., April 23.—The trial of Walter Treadwell, the Southern Kansas cattle king, for the murder of George Clarke, his former partner in the cattle business, which had been in progress here for the past week, closed late Saturday night, and the jury retired with instructions to call the judge at any time if they agreed on a verdict.

Yesterday morning the judge was summoned to the court room by a deputy sheriff and quite a crowd gathered when the report flew around that the jury had agreed. As soon as the judge had taken his seat the jury filed in and in answer to the usual question the foreman announced that they had agreed on a verdict of not guilty. This was received with general approval.

Treadwell, during the trial, proved beyond a shadow of doubt that Clarke had led Mrs. Treadwell astray and that the shooting was committed in the heat of passion caused by his wrongs.

HOLMES ACQUITTED.

MACON, Mo., April 23.—The trial of John Holmes of La Plata, charged with the attempted murder of Mrs. Eliza Nettleton of the same town, was concluded in the circuit court Saturday, the accused being acquitted, as the question of identity was not clearly proved.

Mrs. Nettleton, a respectable and comparatively well-to-do widow, who lived with her daughter at La Plata, where the two kept a boarding house, owned a large farm and employed Holmes to take charge of it. He had on several occasions desired Mrs. Nettleton to grant him her hand in marriage, and her refusal threw him into a great passion. Finally she discharged him and soon after received an anonymous letter threatening her life. To this no attention was paid, but one night in December she awoke and found her throat in the grasp of a masked man who was endeavoring to choke her to death. Her struggles awakened her daughter in an adjoining room, and she in turn alarmed the house, but the man escaped. Holmes was arrested.

A DEADBEAT.

OMAHA, Nob., April 23.—Some time ago a man of attractive presence who introduced himself as Prof. Moranda, came here from Chicago and opened a successful dancing school. Yesterday Prof. Martine, of Chicago, to whom he had referred, arrived for the purpose of arranging for a children's cantata. He at once declared that the alleged Prof. Moranda was Joseph N. Delortie, formerly of Montreal, and more recently of Newark, N. J., and Chicago; that his first wife died from neglect; that he deserted his second and her helpless babe; that he defrauded his father-in-law out of $5,000 and that he was wanted in Newark for passing bogus paper. Prof. Martine says he was also a sufferer to the tune of several hundred dollars, of which he was confined while the man was in his employ in Chicago. Moranda has left the city.

TATE'S DEFALCATION.

LOUISVILLE, Ky., April 23.—The amount of ex-Treasurer Tate's defalcation with all credits made is now placed at $150,000. It is learned that just before leaving he sent the negro porter to the bank for a large sum, saying he wanted it to pay a school claim. As no claims were due this is made evidence that he took with him from $75,000 to $100,000. The commissioners found that the defalcation ran back many years, one of the notes being dated 1868, the year he came into office. In settling from year to year he balanced his books for December 31 and presented his bank balances for the end of the first week in January. In settlements twelve years ago what appear to be forgeries have been found. This crime is extraditable, and it is on account of this that he is believed to be hiding so closely. The I. O. U.'s amount to $50,000. One man has 200. Another sent a check for $100 to meet his, and the check was pinned to the obligation and so will be presented to the Legislature. The bondsmen hope to get off without paying, as several have their property in their wives' names.

MURDER AT MOUSETAIL LANDING.

LOUISVILLE, Ky., April 23.—At Mousetail landing, on the Tennessee river, near Paducah, a man named Ward, who, it is alleged, had been circulating disreputable stories about John Stafford's daughter, was found in a crowd at the landing and, at the pistol point, compelled to c-confess he had lied. Stafford was about to kill him anyhow, but Ward, on his knees, begged for his life and was let off. He went immediately home and, returning with a shotgun, just as Stafford was mounting his horse, shot him dead without a word of warning. Holding the crowd at bay with the other barrel of his gun he backed off and made his escape. It is reported that a band of lynchors is searching for him. One rumor is that he was found yesterday and shot to death.

KILLED HIS MOTHER.

LEMARS, Iowa, April 23.—Philip Beld, a young farmer living fourteen miles west of here, and his mother, who had been on bad terms for some time, quarreled yesterday over seizing a horse, when suddenly Beld fired two shots at his mother, and then went upstairs and shortly after the neighbors heard another shot, and on going up found that he had sent a third bullet into his head. The matricide had always borne a good reputation. His father was killed a year ago by a kick from a horse. The dead woman was forty-seven years old. She had a brother serving a term at Anamosa for manslaughter. The sanity of the family is doubted.

MURDER AT ATLANTA.
Two Negroes Quarrel Over Cards and One Uses His Knife.
ATLANTA, GA., Sept. 29.—Marion Cunningham was cut in the throat by William Merriwether and killed to-night about 8 o'clock in John Ryan's billiard room and saloon on Ivy street. The participants were negroes. They were playing cards for money when a quarrel ensued. After the cutting, Merriweather ran out of the saloon and was pursued by several negroes, who caught him and held him until a policeman arrested him. An inquest was held and a verdict was rendered to the effect that the killing was murder.

One Negro Kills Another in a Dispute Over a Game of Cards.
ATLANTA, Sept. 30.—Last night Jack Ryan's saloon on Ivy street was crowded with negroes. Among those in the room were Marion Cunningham and William Merriwether. These two had been playing a game of five up, in which Cunningham lost money. After the game was over they engaged in an earnest conversation, but no one paid any attention to them until Merriwether, in a loud and angry tone, asked: "Ain't you going to pay the money?"

"No; I haven't the money," answered Cunningham.

"Then I say you are a — scoundrel."s aid Merriwether, so loud that everybody in the hall heard him.

Cunningham made no reply, but turned his head as though intending to walk away. Just as he did so Merriwether jerked his right hand from his pocket, and raising it high above his head, struck Cunningham.

The blow was a hard one, but no one who saw it had any idea that it was a death-dealing one, and no attempt was made to stop the assassin as he he darted through the crowd toward the door. Before he had reached the door, however, those standing nearer Cunningham heard him say:

"My God, he has killed me!"

The murderer was pursued by the mob, determined on lynching him. Chief of Police Conley took steps to prevent the lynching, and hurried Merriwether off to prison. All night long the friends of the dead man lingered around the jail, but were held in check by the police.

TO THE CHAIN-GANG FOR LIFE.
Merriwether Convicted of the Murder of Cunningham.
ATLANTA, GA., Nov. 21.—The trial of the case of William Merriwether, charged with murder for the killing of Marion Cunningham, in a negro billiard saloon last month, by cutting his throat with a knife, which has been on trial in the superior court for several days, was concluded this afternoon. The jury brought in a verdict of guilty, and fixed the penalty at life imprisonment on the chain-gang. Sentence in accordance with the verdict was at once passed by Judge R. H. Clark. The case will be carried to the supreme court.

A Citizen of Sunset Beats and Mistreats His Wife.

Special to the Gazette.

SUNSET, TEX., June 9.—Our quiet little city was thrown into the wildest excitement yesterday evening by the news that Dr. A. N. Willey was attempting to kill his wife. It seems that the Doctor had stripped her of her clothing and was whipping her in an unmerciful manner, which aroused some of the near neighbors. About this time Mrs. Willey succeeded in getting loose from him and was running down the street for her life, and screaming and calling for help and to please not let the doctor kill her. The doctor was following her in hot pursuit with a cocked pistol in his hand, and defying any and everybody to stand back, that he would kill the first man that attempted to check him. The screams and pitiful cries of the poor woman soon brought to her rescue a large number of our citizens. Business men ran hurriedly, leaving their stores open, and soon were at the scene of action. The poor woman, frightened almost to death, ran into a neighbor's house seeking rescue, and the citizens succeeded in catching the Doctor and taking the pistol out of his hands and holding him a prisoner. A complaint was fled against him in the Justice's court for an assault with intent to murder, and his examining trial was set for to-day. After his arrest he abused almost everybody present in a most ridiculous manner. Deputy Sheriffs Norwood and Evans of Bowie arrived about dark and took the prisoner to Montague and placed him in the county jail. The wildest excitement prevailed throughout the town for some time. Mrs. Willey, while she is badly bruised, is able to be up this morning. She is an educated and cultured lady, with a host of warm, personal friends, and all deeply sympathize with her. She has telegraphed to her father, who lives in Tennessee, to come to her relief at the earliest moment.
wylie-gainesville-1888-06-11.A2:
Fatally Beaten by Her Husband.
GAINESVILLE, Tex., June 11.—At Sunset, near here, yesterday, Dr. Wiley, a prominent physician, stripped his wife of all her clothes and beat her unmercifully. She escaped from him and ran through the streets in an entirely nude condition. The doctor pursued her, firing at her from his revolver, but failed to hit her. She sought refuge in a neighbor's house, where the doctor, on attempting to enter, was disarmed and handed over to the officers. He was taken to the Montague jail to prevent lynching by the infuriated citizens. Mrs. Wiley, who is a most estimable lady, will die from the effects of the beating and kicks.

CLARKSVILLE, Tenn., June 12.—[Special.]—This country for miles up and down the river is greatly excited over an epidemic disease of very peculiar character, causing widespread disease and many deaths. Those attacked have symptoms of hydrophobia and die in great agony. The number of deaths in the past ten days in a distance of twenty miles is fifty. It is supposed that the disease is caused by throwing poisoned dogs into the river at Nashville, where several thousand canines have been so disposed of in the past three weeks.

KNOXVILLE, June 12.—[Special.]—Word reached here last night that the Jones-Green war in Hancock county had broken out again. Last Friday John Devault was found murdered. Alleged that he turned traitor to the Jones faction. Saturday a fight occurred in which two of the Jones faction were wounded. Dr. Yee, of Morestown, was called but the Greens warned him away. Saturday night the members of the Jones faction were escorting doctor to home of the wounded when the Green party attacked them.

DOMESTIC.
Northern Minnesota is suffering from a great flood.

Senator Chace of Rhode Island was re-elected Tuesday by the Legislature.

Mr. Depew says he would not decline the Presidential nomination if tendered him.

Governor Hill has vetoed the electoral reform bill enacted by the New York Legislature.

Rev. Dr. James Freeman Clark died at his home in Jamaica Plain, Mass., last Friday night.

The California Republican delegation to Chicago started Sunday evening for the convention.

Severe tempests in Dakota and Michigan on Saturday did a great deal of damage to property and killed several people.

Stephen W. Dorsey says he is a Republican still, and has no intention of opposing any candidate nominated at Chicago.

Mme. Diss DeBar, the notorious confidence woman of New York, was put on trial Monday and was treated to several unpleasant surprises.

The Bell Telephone company is quarreling with the municipal authorities of St. Louis, and threaten to remove their business from that city.

An inhuman physican of Gainesville, Texas, beat his wife unmercifully Monday and drove her naked through the streets. The monster barely escaped lynching.

A Philadelphia woman has confessed to poisoning her two children to get the life insurance. She is also believed to have killed her husband in the same manner.

Jerry Sinclair of Ossipee, N. H., a postal clerk running between Boston and Bangor, was found dead in his car on Saturday evening at the latter city. Whether murder or suicide is not known now.

A dispatch from Chicago says it is considered pretty certain that Warner Miller of New York and John M. Thurston of Nebraska will be temporary chairman and permanent president of the Republican convention, or vice versa.

Four or more desperadoes attempted Friday to rob an express train on the Cincinnati, Indianapolis and St. Louis road, when only 12 miles out of Cincinnati. The baggage master was shot in four places, one robber was killed and the others fled.
